entries.title: Texas Sues Harris County Clerk Over Alleged Targeted Voter Ads
entries.summary: The state accused officials in Harris County — a Democratic stronghold — of promoting voter education ads that targeted specific racial demographics.
entries.content:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s office sued the Harris County Clerk on Thursday to halt a series of get-out-the-vote advertisements, arguing the county had unlawfully targeted Black, Latino and Asian voters.

The lawsuit accuses Teneshia Hudspeth and members of her staff of spending $43,429 on a month’s worth of social media ads through Meta platforms in an effort to target voters by race or ethnicity, claiming that action violated the state constitution. The ads began running on Facebook and Instagram in September and are designed to direct voters to county election resources, according to the complaint.

The suit includes screenshots of the County Election Department’s Meta ad library page, which show the county had prioritized showing ads to users with interests like “African-American literature,” “Hispanic kitchen” and “Latin dance” — tags that purportedly make the posts more discoverable to specific demographic groups.

“Troublingly, these voter awareness ads intentionally target certain racial and ethnic groups,” the complaint says, “but do not target other demographics.”

Paxton is the state’s Republican Senate nominee and faces a tight race against Democrat James Talarico. His office said he has recused himself from the lawsuit because he is on the November ballot.

Hudspeth did not immediately return The Washington Sun’s request for comment. The Harris County clerk’s official Facebook page was still running the ad as of Thursday evening.

Anchored by Houston, Harris County is Texas’ largest county and a Democratic stronghold in the state.

Meta’s ad library website explains that ads can be purchased to reach users based on “age, gender and location,” which may also include “people beyond the targeting criteria but are likely to find an ad relevant.”

State government lawyers are asking a Texas district court to deactivate the ad or have the targeted tags removed, as well as block such targeting in the future.

The attorneys also noted that their request comes a day before early voting ends and five days before Election Day, writing: “Every moment that these advertisements remain active and improperly targeting users based on their race or ethnicity, Defendants are violating the Texas Constitution. But once the 2026 Election is over, the harm will be done (at least, for this series of ads).”

entries.title: El-Sayed and Stevens to Make Rare Joint Appearance in Michigan Senate Race
entries.summary: The former rivals are seeking to show Democratic unity in the tight race ahead of Tuesday's midterms.
entries.content:
By Joey Cappelletti, Corey Williams and Jacqueline Ganun

DETROIT — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed will campaign Sunday in Detroit alongside former primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens, marking their first public appearance together in months after a week in which lingering divisions spilled into public view.

The two will be joined by South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn, one of the country's most prominent Black politicians, at a get-out-the-vote event at a Detroit church, according to two people familiar with the plans who were not authorized to discuss them publicly.

The joint appearance — their first since a Democratic unity breakfast days after the Aug. 4 primary — comes after weeks of Democrats struggling to unite behind El-Sayed after he defeated Stevens by a razor-thin margin. She received significant support from the Jewish and Black communities, leading to concerns about turnout in the general election.

Tensions again spilled into public view Wednesday when Stevens' fiance, Jason Turkish, told The Detroit News that he would vote for Republican Mike Rogers.

Hours later, Stevens appeared on CNN to reaffirm that she would be voting for El-Sayed, but urged his campaign to “shut out the hate and call it out.”

“Make people who are in my coalition, right, make them feel comfortable about coming to the polls,” said Stevens, who drew significant support from Jewish and Black voters during the primary.

El-Sayed's criticism of Israel, past remarks and associations with controversial streamer Hasan Piker have long drawn concern from some in Michigan's large Jewish community. Turkish and others in the Jewish community have said El-Sayed hasn't done enough to address concerns ahead of the general election.

The latest controversy centered on an ad by Rebellion PAC, an independent left-wing group, that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices.

“That has nothing to do with our campaign,” El-Sayed said of the ad. “It’s certainly not what I want to be talking about right now.”

Stevens and other Democrats urged him to go further to denounce the content of the advertisement rather than merely distancing himself from it.

Trump’s rhetoric and actions create challenges for Republicans.


Republicans face political challenges of their own, particularly voter dissatisfaction with Trump, the Iran war and high costs. Rogers has remained closely aligned with the president on most issues, appearing alongside him at a Michigan rally Sunday where he credited Trump with bringing manufacturing jobs back to the state.

The rally took place in Port Huron, just across the river from Canada, a country with deep economic ties to Michigan that Trump has targeted with tariffs.

El-Sayed has held campaign events in heavily Republican areas, including Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. His team also released an ad featuring clips of prominent conservative figures praising him, including former Fox News host Tucker Carlson, who has faced accusations of antisemitism that he denies.

But the ad created another source of friction with some Jewish voters.

Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek in Southfield criticized both the Rebellion PAC ad and El-Sayed’s campaign ad during a call with reporters.

“We are one week away from the election, and it feels like the temperature has turned way up,” Starr said. “Instead of things getting better over the last seven weeks, they’ve actually gotten worse.”

Rogers, meanwhile, appeared Wednesday with Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas at an event hosted by the Republican Jewish Coalition in Birmingham, Michigan. Cruz called antisemitism “a poison that is ripping the country apart” and accused Democrats of being taken over by “self-proclaimed communists and Islamists.”

Trump has repeatedly attacked El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, calling him a “jihadist” and saying Sunday that he was “on the side of terrorists.”

Both campaigns make a final push for Black voters


Both candidates are trying to win over Black voters, particularly in Detroit's Wayne County, where Stevens defeated El-Sayed in the Democratic primary.

El-Sayed is expected to campaign Sunday in the Detroit area with Rep. James Clyburn of South Carolina, part of an effort to shore up support among Black voters. Much of El-Sayed's final campaign stretch has included events in Detroit aimed at increasing turnout.

Rogers has also sought to make inroads with Black voters. He visited a reading remediation program at a Detroit high school and discussed housing costs with residents in Pontiac, north of the city. Earlier this month, his wife handed out $10 gift cards at a gas station.

The gesture drew criticism from Ruby Farmer, a 68-year-old Detroit retiree.

“You’re giving out gas cards in the inner city, you never would come for any other reason,” Farmer said.

While Farmer has a bit of difficulty pronouncing El-Sayed's name, she cast her ballot for him three weeks ago anyways. El-Sayed has come out in opposition to policies by Trump — policies Farmer says directly impact her family.

“I have a special-needs son,” said Farmer. “He depends on Medicaid. Medicaid has been cut, and for home care workers in Michigan all the benefits are on hold.”

___

Cappelletti reported from Washington.

entries.title: Peltola Denies Knowing About Alaska Spoiler Candidate
entries.summary: The Democrat's denial comes as the Justice Department escalates its investigation.
entries.content:
By Becky Bohrer, Meg Kinnard and Alanna Durkin Richer

JUNEAU, Alaska — Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about an effort to put another candidate on the Alaska ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent as the Justice Department escalated a criminal investigation with new grand jury subpoenas.

“I just want to clear the air," she said at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."

Peltola is running against Sen. Dan Sullivan. A person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press that subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan Jr. as part an alleged effort to confuse voters.

The race is considered key to control of the U.S. Senate. More subpoenas were expected, according to the person who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the number of them were immediately clear.

The Justice Department for months has been looking into allegations that Dan J. Sullivan Jr. entered the race to siphon votes from the incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. The potential targets of the investigation are unclear, but President Donald Trump earlier this week called for the criminal prosecution of Peltola and her campaign.

Attorney General Todd Blanche in a Fox News interview on Wednesday said he wouldn’t discuss any criminal investigations, but accused Democrats of “cheating.”

“They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election, not by running on issues but by putting up a person with the same name,” Blanche said.

The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign. “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.

Alaska's Republican governor has also ordered an investigation

Separately, Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into Peltola, saying the newspaper's reporting “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes.”

“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the reporting “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.

Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens," the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. "It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”

Later, as he rallied for Republican Sen. Darline Graham, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted."

Peltola dismisses the claims as a ‘distraction’

Peltola alluded to the controversy in a fundraising post Thursday. “They can’t win on their record so they’re trying to intimidate me into backing down,” she said, adding later: “This is just another distraction as they avoid answering for the skyrocketing cost of living we’re facing because of their tariffs and forever wars. It won’t work.”

In Juneau, Alaska, independent Carter Bancroft said he voted Thursday for Peltola. “I’m very certain in the candidates I wanted to vote for and I wanted to vote for Mary Peltola,” he said.

But he said the latest claims have bothered him. He worries they give “ammunition” to Trump and others to attack Peltola or other Democratic candidates. “And I think I’m bothered by shenanigans on either side," Bancroft said, especially actions intended “to confuse things or try to trick people.”

John Delgado, an independent who leans Republican, said he has “warmed up” to Sen. Sullivan, especially in light of the recent claims. He agrees that Peltola should drop out of the race.

The situation in Alaska isn't that unusual. Political parties often support extra candidates on ballots to try to pull votes from their rivals. If state courts allow it, legal experts say, the federal government has no role challenging the results.

In Ohio’s Senate race, Republicans have been tied to an effort to boost a socialist on the ballot who would pull votes from the Democratic candidate challenging Sen. Jon Husted.

On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance didn’t go as far as Trump did in calling for Peltola to be prosecuted but said he supported a probe into possible election fraud.

“I mean, she is a person who, for months now, has pretended that she has had nothing to do with the fact that they have put a fraudulent person, a person explicitly designed to confuse Alaska voters, on the ballot,” Vance told reporters ahead of a campaign trip to Texas. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful.”

State Supreme Court OK'd the other Sullivan on the ballot

Earlier this year, a top state elections official ruled Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg, ineligible for the primary ballot, concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”

The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.

The New York Times reported that interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit showed Peltola’s team aimed to coax candidates into the race, with the aim of splitting support for the GOP senator.

Asked about the reporting on Wednesday, Trump told journalists, “I think they should be prosecuted.” He earlier had posted on social media that “Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done.”

___

Associated Press writer Seung Min Kim contributed to this report.

entries.title: Thune Says Republicans Have 'Done All We Can Do' Before the Midterms
entries.summary: The Senate majority leader defended his party’s record heading into Election Day, but admits “headwinds” shifted the map.
entries.content:
CLYDE, Ohio — Senate Majority Leader John Thune says he has few regrets about his party’s record and is already waving off fellow Republicans stirring up a blame game about the midterm elections.

Senate Republicans could be days away from losing their majority, with the party needing to suddenly shift big money to red states they believed should have been safe seats.

But on the trail in what has traditionally been a solidly red state, the Republican leader isn’t ready for any Monday morning quarterbacking about what his party could have done differently.

“It's a broader map,” Thune says from the kitchen table of a northern Ohio home. “We've done all we can do, and with the things that we can control.”

When pressed on what’s keeping him up at night, Thune points to the Republican firewall states of Maine, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska. Beyond that, he namechecks Texas, Kansas and Nebraska before acknowledging what he calls “the tough political environment.”

“The president’s not on the ballot, so there's some headwinds that our candidates are dealing with, but they're really high-quality candidates.”

GOP candidates have found themselves on the back foot after months of being battered by the Iran war, and gas and food prices that have remained stubbornly high ever since the conflict began. They’re also dragged down by President Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings that aren’t doing his members much good.

Thune immediately pointed to Sen. Jon Husted, the Republican who is running against former Sen. Sherrod Brown for his first full term and whom Thune is on the road to boost. He's been joined by other prominent Republicans including Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz.
20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_2219.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_1641.jpg (7658x5108, AR: 1.50)Husted, however, is having trouble getting over the hump. Polls show that he and Brown are in a nip-and-tuck race. One unclear factor is whether Vivek Ramaswamy, the party’s candidate for Ohio governor, will drag him down. Ramaswamy’s campaign started cratering after his decision to air a controversial ad featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent who was allegedly sexually abused by her stepfather when she was 12 years old.

Multiple Republicans, including Husted, have argued that the ad was a mistake or that it should be pulled down. Thune indicated that Husted is in the right here.

“I think … there's been enough spent defining candidates in both the governor's race and the Senate races here that I think people are going to be able to differentiate,” Thune said. “I feel really good about our chances here.”

Ohio was among the final stops on the trail for the leader, who campaigned in nearly a dozen places in recent weeks, including in Iowa late last week for Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Senate nominee in another battleground race.

The South Dakota Republican’s lack of second-guessing also applies to the Senate GOP’s response to the unpopular Iran war, which has sent fuel prices soaring. In Ohio, gas prices average $4.26 per gallon, with diesel costs nearing $6.50 per gallon on average.

Thune has sung a consistent tune since the war kicked off in February: that the war should wrap up sooner rather than later, that the Strait of Hormuz should be open and that once the war concludes, prices will normalize. It’s taken longer than he imagined, but he defends his party sticking behind the Trump administration’s strategy.

“I don't think we were in a position, frankly, that we could have done anything differently. As I look back on the last year … in the category of things that we can control, I think we did everything we possibly could,” Thune said. “When you're in a situation like that, where you've got troops deployed in harm's way, everybody kind of surrounds the flag and makes sure that we stick together for the country.  Now, I'm hopeful that the president and his team will bring this to a fairly quick end. I feel like we're getting there.”

Whether that happens remains to be seen. The White House has indicated to allies in the Middle East that a “short, intense military campaign” against Iran is expected once the midterms conclude, according to The Wall Street Journal.

As for his own political future, Thune is expected to run for a second term leading the Republican conference, despite some discontent among members on his right flank.
20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_2699.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)There are a number of questions in the leadership race, including whether Trump will get involved one way or another. Thune recently told CBS News that he isn’t banking on Trump’s support.

Helping Thune out is that there is no obvious challenger at this point.

“[Thune] doesn’t hire senators. He doesn’t fire senators. He doesn’t set our pay. He can’t reprimand us. Other than that, he’s the leader,” Ohio’s other Republican senator, Bernie Moreno, told The Sun with a laugh during an interview. “It’s a thankless job. He does a great job.”

“He’s an incredible human being. Probably too nice sometimes,” Moreno said. “But look, he’s going to be the leader of the conference one way or the other. Nobody’s running against him, and I think that’s the way it should be.”

But Thune has found himself on the wrong side of some of Trump’s MAGA allies and his own colleagues who demanded he pass the SAVE America Act, the hardline voting bill that has no avenue of passage in the upper chamber.

Some of those backers are already laying the groundwork to blame the Senate Republican leader if the midterms go south for the party. Unsurprisingly, Thune is used to the constant criticism.

“They blame me for everything,” he said. “You got people out there … they're going to complain when their ice cream's cold. There's just a lot of people who are never gonna be happy.”

On top of an already-brewing blame game, Thune is also preparing for what could be an onerous lame duck session, especially if Republicans lose the chamber. Leading the to-do list is funding the government, a defense authorization bill and farmer’s assistance legislation. He is also eyeing a permitting reform bill that is set to be the first item to hit the floor during the two-month work session, pending Democratic cooperation.

The big “if” remains whether a third budget reconciliation package is on the agenda, especially if this marks the final weeks of the Republican trifecta. Moreno recently told reporters that losing control in Congress would prompt a “last supper” vehicle for the party to cram in priorities of all stripes, but it’s unclear what could pass.

“Right now, we don't have the votes to get on a third recon bill [and a] budget resolution. … We might have them after [the midterms],” Thune said. “We don’t have it now, and we don’t know that we have the votes to defend against the poison pill Democrat amendments.”
20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_5032.jpg (8145x5433, AR: 1.50)20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_5132.jpg (8136x5427, AR: 1.50)He said there are unknown factors: “The question is, how does the election outcome change that? I think the election outcome obviously is probably going to shape in a very significant way what's achievable in the lame duck.” He also admitted, “it's going to be the art of the doable.”

While talk in the immediate term focuses on his future as leader, questions have also risen about how long Thune plans to stick around the Capitol.

He took a full year to decide whether to run for a fourth term in 2022. But he has already indicated that he will seek a fifth term in 2028, with an official announcement likely to come sooner rather than later.

“We'll start putting the wheels in motion fairly quickly on that,” he said about a timeline for a decision. Referring to his critics on the right, he said, “obviously, there's all this speculation that they'll come after me and want to primary me. They did that last time.”

“I'm fully confident that we can survive both primary and general elections, but it's got to be the right thing to do,” Thune continued. “That's always a conversation my wife and I have — kind of about where we are in life, and where we think we can make the biggest difference, and I feel like the job I have right now is a bit of a calling.”

entries.title: Trump Administration Halts Funding for Key Ukraine Security Programs
entries.summary: State Department officials told congressional staff last month that the White House had sent guidance to stop future aid from being released.
entries.content:
The Trump administration has halted future aid to Ukraine through the International Narcotics Control and Law Enforcement program, even as Russia intensifies attacks on the country's energy infrastructure ahead of winter.

During a late-September meeting with congressional staff, State Department officials said they had received White House guidance to stop future funding through the program, according to a Senate Democratic aide familiar with the discussion. The INCLE program helps Ukraine's police, border guards and other security personnel protect civilians and critical infrastructure.

The guidance from the White House came despite the State Department's earlier decision to allow Ukraine's INCLE programs to continue after the agency completed a foreign assistance review. State later redirected $50 million in congressionally appropriated fiscal year 2025 funding intended for Ukraine to the Western Hemisphere, the aide said.

The department did not notify Congress of the transfer, according to the aide. The State Department divided the $50 million among several Western Hemisphere countries in amounts below congressional notification thresholds, according to the aide, who said the transfers were structured to avoid notifying Congress.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-New Hampshire), the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) are pressing Secretary of State Marco Rubio to release urgently needed security assistance to Ukraine and prevent another diversion of congressionally approved funding.

In a bipartisan letter to Rubio shared with The Washington Sun, the senators said State had “inexplicably reprogrammed” the $50 million and demanded an explanation. They also urged Rubio to prioritize Ukraine when distributing $80 million in fiscal year 2026 INCLE funding designated for Europe and Eurasia. Congress did not earmark the entire amount for Ukraine.

"Delaying the obligation of FY 2026 funds risks leaving Ukrainian citizens and infrastructure more vulnerable at a critical moment," the senators wrote.

Russia has intensified attacks on Ukraine's energy facilities ahead of winter, threatening electricity, heating and water supplies for millions of Ukrainians.

Congressional staff said they are concerned the administration could again redirect funds intended for Ukraine to the Western Hemisphere.

The State Department has separately redirected roughly $52 million in Foreign Military Financing intended for European and Middle Eastern partners to the Western Hemisphere, drawing criticism from Shaheen and New York Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

Shaheen and Tillis also argued that continued assistance to Ukraine would strengthen its anti-corruption institutions and rule of law, helping create a more stable environment for American businesses operating in the country.

They pointed to approximately 120 American companies operating in Ukraine and said cooperation with Ukrainian security institutions also gives the U.S. access to lessons from the country's rapidly evolving defense technology.

entries.title: Cole Hutson Scores Twice In Caps’ 4-3 Win Over the Predators
entries.summary: Boone Jenner and Alex Tuch also scored and Charlie Lindgren made 25 saves for Washington, which has won three games in a row.
entries.content:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Cole Hutson scored twice to lead the Washington Capitals to a 4-3 victory over the Nashville Predators on Thursday night.

Boone Jenner and Alex Tuch also scored and Charlie Lindgren made 25 saves for Washington, winners of three straight and five of six. Aliaksei Protas and Jack St. Ivany each had two assists.

Filip Forsberg scored twice, Ross Colton also scored and Juuse Saros made 25 saves for Nashville, losers of four of five. Roman Josi had three assists.

Forsberg opened the scoring with 7:12 left in the first period.

With the Predators on a 5-on-3, Ryan O’Reilly sent a pass from the high slot to Forsberg at the top of the left circle, where he beat Lindgren with a one-timer.

Forsberg has scored a power-play goal in three-straight games. O’Reilly extended his points streak to four games. He has three goals and four assists over that span.

Hutson tied it with 3:47 left on the first with a sharp angle shot from near the goal line on the right side.

Jenner gave Washington a 2-1 lead at 4:15 of the second.

Forsberg struck again at 9:09 of the second, avoiding a Lindgren poke check before slipping the puck inside the right post for his second of the game.

It was Forsberg’s first multi-goal game of the season.

Hutson scored his second of the game with 6:14 to go in the second, skating through the slot and beating Saros with a wrist shot on the stick side for the first two-goal game of his career.

Colton tied it at 3 at 6:34 of the third, but Tuch scored the winner with 9:51 remaining on a wrist shot from the left faceoff dot for his 10th of the season and fifth goal in his last three games.

Up Next

Capitals: Host Minnesota on Sunday.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: White Out
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Oct. 30, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: The delegate’s decision, trash talk and a call for your best D.C.-themed Halloween costumes.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 9/10: Plenty of sunshine, highs from near 70 to the mid-70s and low humidity. Only a gusty breeze keeps it from perfection. Read the full forecast.

THE LATEST

It’s official: Robert White will resign from his role on the D.C. Council effective Monday to remain eligible in the race for D.C. congressional delegate.

“I made the decision this afternoon after hearing from many residents who expressed their hope that I would represent them in Congress,” White said in a statement yesterday evening. “Their trust means a great deal to me, and I wanted to remove any doubt before Election Day about my eligibility to serve as Delegate.”

The at-large council member told reporters just one day prior that he would continue exploring remedies to his eligibility status. The issue hinges on the interpretation of a 1970 law that requires that the delegate cannot hold another paid public position at the time of their election, complicating a race White was all but certain to clinch as the Democratic nominee.

But White previously told The Washington Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler that he and D.C.’s attorney general differ on their reading of that provision. He thought he had to resign by early December, when the election is certified, but the AG thought it meant Nov. 3. Republican nominee for delegate, Denise Rosado, thinks he’s already disqualified since early voting is underway.

Clearly, though it’s thrown the future of some of his housing bills into the air just as the council period is coming to a close, White has decided to hedge his bets.

“I’m not going to jeopardize going into Congress,” he previously told The Sun.

Council Chair Phil Mendelson’s office told Michael earlier this week that the chairman will take on White’s staff until the end of the calendar year, the usual policy when there is an unexpected council member absence.

“I have an incredibly capable team who will remain at the Council through the end of the year and work with my Council colleagues to get our bills passed. They understand the urgency of the housing challenges residents face and share my commitment to following through on the work we’ve started,” White told The Sun.





DEEP DIVE

D.C. is out of its most commonly used trash cans. The city’s department of public works ordered more of its 96-gallon “supercans” in August, but a supply chain issue has delayed their getting into residents’ hands, The Sun’s Zara Norman reports.

More are en route, interim department director Chris Rodriguez said, and should arrive within the next 7 to 10 days. But the delay — which is around typical for the agency, according to a 2025 performance oversight report — has rankled some residents who’ve been waiting for months.

“I do not understand how the city can simply be out of trash cans,” one Ward 3 resident wrote The Sun in an email. “The city requires that residents use these particular cans for trash pick-up and requires residents to pay for these cans.”

Adding to that anxiety? D.C.’s eternal nemesis, the rat, which tends to chew through city cans.

“Although this seems to be a relatively small matter, trash disposal is a vital basic city service, and is important to the safety and quality of life of all residents, especially given the massive and growing rat problem throughout the city,” the Ward 3 resident wrote.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Nickel and dimed: A class action lawsuit filed yesterday alleges that major D.C. landlord Vivmark Residential, which owns more than 5,300 units in D.C., illegally charged tenants excessive “junk” fees for services that should have been included in rent, like trash removal or having keyless doors, Zara reports.

Closing (tee) time: The National Park Service intends to close East Potomac Park by Nov. 15 to begin the planned redevelopment to turn the golf course there into a “world class championship” facility, The Sun’s Justice Covert and Gavin J. Quinton report.

Today at 10 a.m., Trump administration lawyers will explain to U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes what its plans are regarding the closure and provide details on when President Donald Trump directed the Interior Department and NPS to shutter the course.

A lively policy debate over the District’s purse strings unfolded Thursday after D.C. Auditor Kathy Patterson floated an early stage proposal to abolish the independent chief financial officer and return the role to the executive branch, Michael reports. Patterson argued the setup is an “expensive hindrance” that fails to stop agency overspending, prompting Mendelson to defend the office as a vital guardrail.

Mayor Muriel Bowser is on her way out, and neighborhood blog Popville landed the first interview in her departure tour. She talks about her proudest accomplishment over 12 years in office, says D.C. needs to be more accommodating of local restaurants and businesses, admits to avoiding most social media, and more.





FROM VIRGINIA

The mystery buyer of an Arlington credit union and Crossfit gym has pitched turning the building into a “first of its kind” car wash manned by robots, the Washington Business Journal reports. The facility would apparently clean both the exterior and interior of up to 22 vehicles at a time in 22 separate bays.





FROM MARYLAND

A Maryland woman faces 38 counts of fraud and theft after billing the D.C. Medicaid program for services she didn’t actually provide, resulting in fraudulent payments of $109,000, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.





TRICK OR TREAT

It’s Halloween tomorrow, and we want to see all your D.C.-themed costumes and home decor. Email us at metro@washsun.com by Sunday evening for a chance to be featured in a very spooky edition of the Metro newsletter.





METRO MOMENT


2027NCBF_OfficialArtwork_hires_withlegal copy.jpg (3885x5730, AR: 0.68)
We may just be adjusting to the fall, but there’s reason to look forward to the spring.

This week the organizers of the National Cherry Blossom Festival unveiled details about next year’s 100th annual celebration — including the festival’s official artwork. Produced by D.C.-born artist Chris Pyrate — who has worked with the Wizards and Metro — the piece shows the Tidal Basin awash in both pink cherry blossoms and references to the city’s dual identities.

“There’s a lot of things here that call back to D.C. culture and the international presence in the city,” he said, pointing to Japanese dancers, our famed pandas, Anacostia’s Big Chair, go-go legend Chuck Brown and local culinary staple mambo sauce.

The festival will run from March 20 to April 11, 2027.


SPORTS

Twenty-five years before Caps star Alex Ovechkin embarked on his final-season farewell tour, another “Great 8” had the chance to go out on his own terms. Orioles legend Cal Ripken spoke with The Sun’s Dave Sheinin (who covered Ripken’s final year) about what Ovie can expect.

“First of all, your priority is always to the game,” Ripken said. “Focus on the game, prepare yourself for the game. But beyond that, go ahead and let yourself surrender to it — to the acknowledgment of you and what you meant to the sport.”

“When you’re sitting in that rocking chair — which some of the teams actually gave me as sort of a joke — and you’re thinking back, you think of it fondly,” Ripken added. “Going out [of the sport] can be a wonderful, positive experience.” Read Dave’s full story here.

Wizards rookie AJ Dybantsa looked like a veteran in his NBA debut, The Sun’s Alex Schiffer writes. Alex also heard from other former No. 1 overall picks on what Dybantsa can expect.

entries.title: Morning Sun: High Hopes
entries.content:
Today’s notice: The battleground map is getting very busy, and very big. Trump campaigns from home. Democrats press the Pentagon on Iran war deaths. And: A bipartisan request for answers on Ukraine aid.

The Washington Sun has a new newsletter starting Nov. 9: Congressional reporters Igor Bobic and Oriana González are taking you inside the Capitol in The Stakeout. Sign up now.





THE MAP

Democrats’ expectations are as high as they can be heading into the final weekend before the midterms. We have stories below of a Democratic governor playing in a Trump +38 district and more party money flowing to Senate races in South Carolina and Mississippi of all places. At this point, if Democrats don’t win the Senate, many will see it as a failure. Are their hopes too lofty?

“If we continue fighting in more and more and more states, and we don’t win ’em all, we’ll still win a bunch,” Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear told us in New Mexico this week.

Another potential 2028er, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, told us the risk to the narrative is worth the reward — while campaigning for the longest of Democratic long shots, Mississippi Senate nominee Scott Colom. “We are expanding the map for a reason, and we should lean into that,” Buttigieg said. “I think the knowledge and the muscle memory of how to have those conversations and expand the coalition is actually a very healthy thing to have more of inside the party, too.”

Still, the bar for a good night has been set very high. Too high for some. “To steal some phrasing I heard earlier today, I think the party is nauseously optimistic,” Rodericka Applewhaite of Majority Democrats told The Washington Sun’s Jasmine Wright. “No one seriously thinks a double chamber sweep is a done deal.”

From the emotional roller coaster both parties are riding now:

Ohio: John Thune talks to The Sun. “We’ve done all we can do, and with the things that we can control,” the Senate majority leader told our Al Weaver on a campaign stop in Clyde. What keeps Thune up at night? Maine, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska, Texas, Kansas and Nebraska, he told Al. “The president’s not on the ballot, so there’s some headwinds that our candidates are dealing with,” he said, “but they’re really high-quality candidates.”

Alaska: Dan Sullivan-gate is already an ad. “Alaskans Won’t Fall for Peltola’s Scheme” is the title of the newest spot from the NRSC. The ad is basically a negative campaign ad-style recounting of what the NRSC called the “bombshell New York Times investigation” into how that other Dan Sullivan got on the ballot alongside Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

“I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Democrat Mary Peltola told a crowd in Juneau yesterday. “That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”

Texas: State sues Harris County over too woke GOTV ad targeting. The office of Attorney General Ken Paxton (who just so happens to be the Republican nominee for Senate) accused county clerk Teneshia Hudspeth’s office of running nonpartisan voting information ads online that “intentionally target certain racial and ethnic groups,” meaning Black, Latino and Asian voters, “but do not target other demographics,” i.e. white people.

Kansas: The next House map expansion. The DCCC is putting up its first TV ad in the 2nd Congressional District today, The Sun’s Kadia Goba reports. KS-02 was a Trump +20 district in 2024.

Pennsylvania: Josh Shapiro’s project. He took his gubernatorial campaign into deep-red turf yesterday, campaigning for Democratic House candidate Rachel Wallace in a Trump +38 district. Wallace is trying to unseat Republican Rep. Dan Meuser. “We have not gotten support from the national Democratic Party,” Wallace told The Sun’s Alex Roarty on the trail yesterday. “But I have gotten support from Josh Shapiro. And that means a lot to me, and it means a lot to our community.”

Michigan: Together again. After a week of fiancé-gate following Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens’ betrothed endorsing Republican Mike Rogers over Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, the two former Democratic primary rivals will appear on stage together Sunday. They will be joined at a rally by Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina).

The Sun’s Christa Dutton reports from an El-Sayed rally last night with Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin (who has been a much more vocal supporter than Stevens has been). Someone in the crowd told Christa they see El-Sayed as “Obama number two.”

South Carolina: Ralph Norman spoiler? Much of the past week or so in this Senate race has been about a man not on the ballot — Norman, the conservative congressman who lost to Sen. Darline Graham in the Republican primary and won’t campaign with her (and whose son has said he may vote for Democratic nominee Annie Andrews). Now there are signs an organized write-in campaign for Ralph Norman is gaining steam. Donald Trump stumped with Graham in Norman’s district yesterday, but NewsNation reported that Norman said he was not invited and would not have gone even if he was.

Alabama: Dummymander watch. The 2nd Congressional District — which Republicans redrew especially to oust Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures — is proving to be very competitive. Larry Sabato’s Crystal Ball rated the race a “toss-up” this week, and the NRCC and Republican nominee Rhett Marques dropped their first coordinated ad buy worth $13,565.

North Carolina: The most expensive House race, as in of all time, is in the state’s 1st District, where AdImpact says more than $54 million in ad reservations have been purchased this cycle. The new district map — redrawn by Republicans to boost their own chances — means the 1st now covers basically the entire northeast of the state. Democratic Rep. Don Davis is vying to keep his seat against Republican Laurie Buckhout.

Illinois: The pope votes by mail. “Robert Francis Prevost is on the list of individuals who requested a vote by mail ballot for the upcoming election,” the American pope’s county clerk, Kim Fladhammer, told the Chicago Sun-Times.

Nevada: A donation from beyond the grave? Republican David Flippo’s campaign recorded a donation of $143.56 from Val Sheldon on Oct. 13, though a woman matching the information listed died in 2019, The Sun’s Jenna Monnin reports. Flippo’s campaign treasurer said he is “looking into it.” It was not the first time Flippo’s campaign has recorded a contribution from a dead person.

More: Democrats Have a Bogeyman in Musk. They’re Hardly Using Him. • Ramaswamy Pulls Controversial Ad Featuring His Opponent’s Estranged Mother • Judge Wants More Details on Trump Administration’s Noncitizen Voting Pressure Campaign • Meet America’s Most Political Sports Owners





FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


Trump drops his travel plans: “Must be some bad internals,” one MAGA strategist tells us after the president canceled rallies in Kansas and Iowa over the weekend in favor of virtual appearances. “The telerallies are such a cop out and don’t do anything. In the 2022 cycle, they started doing them and candidates hated it.”

Don’t read anything into this, insists the White House. “Standing up telerallies allows him to hit EVERYWHERE with everything tightening. There will be over 20 telerallies before Election Day,” an administration official told The Sun.

More: Trump Talks to Grok. Democrats Plan to Find Out What He’s Saying.





FROM THE PENTAGON


Dems demand an accurate Iran war toll: Five House Democrats are pressing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for a full account of American casualties in the Iran war, accusing the Pentagon of intentionally misleading the public. DOD says the death toll is 22; other reports have it at 23.

“The public deserves to know the true cost of this war,” Reps. Marcy Kaptur, Susie Lee, Stephen Lynch, Raja Krishnamoorthi and Joe Morelle wrote in a letter obtained by The Sun’s Joe Gould.

More: WSJ: Top Military Admiral Briefs Trump on Iran Options





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Senators press for answers on Ukraine aid: The Trump administration has halted money flowing to Ukraine for a program helping with police, border guards and other security personnel — money the State Department has apparently diverted to the Western Hemisphere, The Sun’s Hamed Ahmadi reports. Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (D-New Hampshire) and Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) are asking why the funds were “inexplicably reprogrammed” and say the move “risks leaving Ukrainian citizens and infrastructure more vulnerable at a critical moment.”



More: Forget Banning Stock Trades. A Democratic Majority Must Tackle All Corruption.

entries.title: The Caps Wanted to Honor Ovechkin — And the Victory Visor Was Born
entries.summary: When deciding how they wanted to celebrate each other after wins this year, the Capitals settled on something that would celebrate Ovechkin, too.
entries.content:
Two weeks ago, Vincent Desharnais became the first Capitals player this season to be named “Legend of the Game,” an honor bestowed upon one key contributor after each win.

His first thought was: Man, it’s dark in here.

The award comes in the form of an old helmet with a mirrored visor, á la what Alex Ovechkin wore in 2005, when he was a rookie quick to deliver on all the promises made about his audacious skill. It’s been a long time. Visors like these are now banned by the International Ice Hockey Federation and have not been seen in the NHL in years. The 30-year-old Desharnais had never been around one. So while the defenseman was soaking in the moment, teammates cheering while he donned the helmet for his role in a 4-2 win over the Devils, he was also marveling at the lack of light.

Ovi could see in a visor like this? 

“Actually putting it on, it’s very tinted — like, very, very dark,” Desharnais said. “It’s mind-blowing that he was able to play with that.”

This is the 21st and final NHL season for 41-year-old Ovechkin. He’s insisted that he does not want much fuss around his farewell. But that insistence has sometimes been met with resistance. When his teammates considered how they wanted to celebrate each other after wins this year, they settled on something that would celebrate Ovechkin, too.

And maybe poke a little fun at just how long the star has been around.

“For the players to have their own thing that really means something to them, and they can laugh about and appreciate, I think is always great,” Capitals coach Spencer Carbery told The Washington Sun. “I thought it was just very fitting.”

Washington has cycled through various celebratory postgame items over the years. An Abraham Lincoln-esque hat and beard. (“The Honest Abe Players’ Player of the Game.”) A yellow rope. (This one came from Arlington County Fire Station No. 2, near the Capitals’ practice facility, meant to suggest all working toward the same goal: “Pulling on the same rope.”) A karate-style headband known as a hachimaki. (Former head coach Peter Laviolette watched a lot of “Cobra Kai” during the pandemic.)

Some years come and go without any postgame items. The Capitals did not have one last year. Carbery does not like to press his own ideas if the players do not find one of their own: “I’ve always encouraged players to organically come up with something,” he said. “I don’t think it’s something that the coach forces.”

His team did not take long to settle on something this year. The players knew they wanted something connected to Ovechkin.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“He’s a legend,” said forward Tom Wilson, the longest-tenured member of the roster besides Ovechkin and his only remaining teammate from the 2018 Stanley Cup. “It just seemed pretty fitting to do something to pay tribute to him in his last season.”

The Capitals have four wins since introducing the helmet and visor on Oct. 17. Desharnais has been joined so far in receiving the honor by Alex Tuch, Jack St. Ivany and Cole Hutson.
Tuch_Helmet_2 copy.jpg (3129x2086, AR: 1.50)Wilson led the charge on brainstorming with player leadership. He was adamant the item should be something to honor Ovechkin. The idea of the old mirrored visor came from forward Anthony Beauvillier: “It just popped in my head,” he said. Washington hockey operations and equipment staff helped track down the right gear.

Ovechkin burst into the league two decades ago with a flashy style to match his game. The electric yellow laces. The perpetually tucked jersey. And, of course, the mirrored visor, which shielded the upper half of his face in a way vaguely reminiscent of RoboCop.

It quickly became a point of controversy. Opponents hated that it covered his eyes and made it harder to anticipate his movement with the puck. NHL marketing executives reportedly felt similarly — not because they believed the visor offered a competitive advantage but because they wanted fans to see as much of the young star as often as possible. Including his eyes.

After his rookie season, in June 2006, the league brought a potential ban of mirrored visors to a vote among general managers.

The GMs voted 29-1 in favor of a ban. The lone dissenting vote, naturally, was then-Capitals GM George McPhee.

Ultimately, the league did not follow through with codifying that ban into the rule book. But Ovechkin didn’t push it, and retired the mirrored visor anyway. (He eventually had to give up his tucked jersey, too, when the NHL tweaked its uniform rules in 2013. The yellow laces, of course, are still here.) Now, all these years later, in search of an item to symbolize what Ovechkin brought to the sport, his teammates knew what to choose.

“It was just, Can we get the helmet done? Can we get the visor done? And then hockey ops and our trainers and everyone sourced the stuff,” Wilson said. “It came together.”
1080p 24fps.00_26_39_12.Still100 copy.jpg (1620x1080, AR: 1.50)Capitals staff fixed up an old helmet and found a visor in storage. (This one was not worn on the ice by Ovechkin in 2005 but is nearly identical to what he did wear.) Many of the current players are too young to have any original memories of the gear.

Some were not even born when Ovechkin entered the league. That includes Ilya Protas, who is now his linemate. (Earlier this season, when 20-year-old Protas scored on an assist from Ovechkin for the first time, the young forward was so excited that he took home the stick to save it.) Ovechkin’s future head coach was still in college: Carbery watched Ovechkin’s historic rookie campaign as a senior at D-III St. Norbert in Wisconsin. (“I remember thinking, Whoa, that’s interesting,” Carbery said of the mirrored visor. “It reminded me of the running backs in the NFL.”) Even the helmet itself is clearly a throwback from another era.

“Guys, I’m still young, by the way,” Ovechkin joked when Wilson presented him with the helmet in front of the team for the first time. The captain briefly placed it on his own head. Then he took it off and passed it on.

entries.title: Democrats Have a Bogeyman in Musk. They’re Hardly Using Him.
entries.summary: The world’s richest man is likely to be the midterm election’s largest spender, but most Democrats have set their attention elsewhere.
entries.content:
Elon Musk is likely to end this election cycle as the biggest single donor. He’s also surprisingly hard to find.

The last time Elon Musk got involved in an election, last year in Wisconsin, he was everywhere: He spent millions of dollars and danced onstage before a crowd of thousands wearing a block of foam cheese on his head. His chosen candidate lost by 10 percentage points. Wisconsin Democrats used Musk’s involvement in the state Supreme Court race as fodder for advertisements, and now they credit voters’ irritation with Musk for boosting turnout and making a potentially pivotal difference in the special election.

This year, the richest man in the world has avoided campaign trail theatrics, even as he’s upped his financial stake.

Musk isn’t doing a disappearing act on his own: relative to last year, most Democrats have shown little interest in demonizing the trillionaire who is spending against them. The key exception is in Texas, where Musk’s presence as a business owner and megadonor have resulted in his being inextricably linked to Republican downballot races.

“Trump and the Republican candidates are doing so badly now on the economy, on gas, that you don't need to have a secondary or an outside bogeyman to gin people up,” Eddie Vale, a Democratic strategist, told The Washington Sun. “If gas was a dollar cheaper a gallon, if we weren't at war in Iran … I think then you would have seen more anti-Elon stuff.”

The Sun’s analysis of AdImpact data showed that since Sept. 1, 37 unique ads mentioning Musk by name ran in federal-level races, costing $2.7 million. During the same period, 351 ads ran that addressed corruption, costing $176 million; $56 million was spent on 189 ads discussing the economy.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read.

Musk has spent at least $276 million supporting Republican candidates so far this cycle — some analysis of Federal Election Commission data puts the number above $400 million. Most of that money has been funneled through political action committees, like the Senate Leadership Fund and America PAC, which Musk founded in 2024.

Musk did not respond to request for comment.

FEC filings show that America PAC alone has spent millions on mailers, text messages and phone calls in key battleground races, with the highest spending aiding Senate races: $1.5 million to support Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, $2.3 million for Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa, close to $6 million for former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan and nearly $7.6 million for Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio.

On the other side of those races, the Democratic candidates have honed in on messages about affordability and corruption in Washington. They haven’t spent much time invoking Musk’s name, and they may not need to.

Ben Wikler, the former chair of the Wisconsin Democrats, said the Wisconsin election showed that “Elon Musk is bad” isn’t a winning message on its own. The party’s highest-rated advertisement of the cycle connected an ongoing case Musk had before the state Supreme Court to his interest in installing a conservative judge.

“When you connect the dots and point out that if he's able to buy a victory for these politicians, then they're going to do him favors that are going to cost [voters] money, that's when it really clicks,” Wikler said.

In Texas, Senate candidate James Talarico is one Democrat attempting to do just that. Musk, who moved to Texas in 2020, is actively pursuing land deals in the state for SpaceX and data centers; Talarico has seized on those deals and has accused Musk of attempting to “buy a senator” who will be indebted to him.

On the campaign trail, Talarico prominently uses Musk as an example of the type of corruption voters are concerned about.

“If you’ve received a text message saying scary things about me, that was Elon,” Talarico said during a campaign speech earlier this month. “Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our taxpayer dollars.”

America PAC has spent nearly $34 million in support of Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton. Musk has routed an additional $190 million into the race, The Texas Tribune reports, through donations to the Senate Leadership Fund.

Musk has also attacked Talarico on social media, posting last week “there is something deeply wrong” with the Democrat.

“There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal U.S. Senator,” Talarico responded.

Katherine Fischer of the Democratic Texas Majority PAC said she believes that Musk may be a figure that can galvanize voters in Texas like he did in Wisconsin last year. In speeches, ads and online, Talarico has found ways to link Musk’s presence in the state to three of the leading issues voters care about: affordability, data centers and corruption, she said.

And at a time when voters are frustrated by rising costs, Fischer said she believes it is “wise” for candidates in the state to emphasize how much Musk is spending on the conservative ballot.

“There's a certain pride in Texas around liberty and choice,” Fischer said. “Watching the richest man in the world come in and try to buy a Senate seat. … It's not a good story for [Republicans], and I understand why the Dems are going after it.”

Musk’s connection to data centers has made him a character in other races. In New York’s competitive 17th Congressional District, Democrat Cait Conley has pointed to Musk’s financial support for her competitor, Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, and past Lawler statements that have been seen as favorable to data center development.

Conley accused Lawler of being a “puppet” for Musk during an appearance on CNN. America PAC has spent $500,000 in support of Lawler. A source close to the Conley campaign told The Sun that Conley chose to bring up Musk because voters in the district have felt a “tangible impact” from data center development in the area, and they saw a clear tie between the issue and “who or what is bankrolling” Lawler.

The Lawler campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

But in states where Musk’s presence isn’t as overtly felt, Democrats may be right to remind voters that it is Republicans, not Musk, who are on the ballot. The Musk “line of attack” may not be as effective as other areas where Republicans are failing, Wikler said.

“If voters are telling you every hour or every day that grocery prices are their top concern, then don’t stop talking about grocery prices in order to lean into Elon Musk,” he said.

entries.title: Forget Banning Stock Trades. A Democratic Majority Must Tackle All Corruption.
entries.summary: New lawmakers won’t settle for just one reform, and will demand more aggressive steps.
entries.content:
The 120th Congress is setting up for a collision course on how far to push an ethics agenda meant to signal to voters that lawmakers heard their concerns about corruption in Washington.

On one side of the debate will be longtime members of Congress who will try to placate the hunger for so-called reform with proposals that would limit the owning or trading of stocks by lawmakers, or outright ban the practices.

But on the other side will be the dozens and dozens of new members who have aggressively campaigned on a more sweeping agenda and argue a stock ban should merely be an opening act early next year.

They are pushing for additional measures, including a lifetime ban on members becoming lobbyists after leaving Congress, tougher criminal sentences for lawmakers found violating public trust, a ban on joining corporate boards after leaving office, and even the adoption of term limits.

“Going to Congress should be sort of the pinnacle of what you do in your life as a public servant. You know, it shouldn't be a stepping stone to getting a job somewhere else,” Bob Harvie, a Democrat running against a 10-year incumbent in the Philadelphia suburbs, told The Washington Sun last month.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read.

Even Sherrod Brown, the Ohio Democrat trying to return to the Senate after a 32-year run in Congress ended in defeat in 2024, has made bashing today’s lawmakers on Capitol Hill a central plank of his stump speeches, promising to limit their financial opportunities.

“They’re betting on those stocks going up and down as they vote for legislation on the Senate and House floor. And then many of them, after they quit, they become lobbyists,” Brown told a couple hundred carpenters at a rally outside Toledo two weeks ago. “So here's the thing: If you run for office and you can't promise you won’t trade stocks, if you can’t promise you won't be a lobbyist, you’ve got no business holding public office.”

Brown drew a 15-second ovation from the union workers, the longest of his 17-minute speech.

Promising to change Washington is not new. In 1994, then-Rep. Newt Gingrich of Georgia drew up the “Contract with America,” vowing to end Congress’ “cycle of scandal and disgrace.” In 2006, when Republicans controlled Congress, Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-California) promised ethics changes to “drain the swamp” and end a “culture of corruption.” Democrats made the same promises in 2018.

But those were agenda proposals drawn up in Washington by teams advising the speaker-in-waiting, leading to extensive proposals and legislative debates in early 1995, 2007 and 2019, respectively.

This year, Democrats have not embraced a national agenda, and ethics proposals have ranged all over the map. Should they win the majority, most Democratic leaders are focused on trying to change some provisions governing the House that will pass in a rules package on the first or second day of the new Congress. Work on a broader ethics overhaul would come later in the spring.

“I don’t think final decisions are made, but we’re working to ensure that we can do the most possible. But people should be prepared for us to address these issues,” California Rep. Pete Aguilar, the No. 3 Democratic leader, told The Washington Sun’s Daniella Diaz during a campaign swing in Texas this week.

Aguilar, likely to become majority whip if Democrats win, called a stock ban a “big piece” of the ethics proposals to be considered.

But voters want a lot more on corruption issues, and Democratic candidates have heard that at rallies and seen it vividly in their focus groups and internal polling of swing voters.

Over two months last winter, House Majority PAC, a super PAC aligned with Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, conducted surveys about inflation and corruption. Global Strategy Group, the Democratic polling firm, asked voters who was to blame for high costs: “out of touch politicians” or corporations that “continued to jack up prices."

By a 2-to-1 margin, voters blamed politicians.

There was statistically almost no difference in blame laid on politicians by Democratic voters (70%), independents (68%) and Republicans (63%), according to an HMP memo.

The PAC’s opposition researchers used the data to rework the files on incumbent Republicans who had won close races before, and they shaped messages to take advantage of the sentiment about dirty politicians. Over the next few months, Democratic challengers began running ads against incumbents tying everything from stock trades to donations from companies tied to data centers to corruption and higher prices.

Democrats like Shannon Taylor placed her ethics agenda at the top of her website, bringing back the old promise to end the “culture of corruption.” She’s campaigning against Rep. Rob Wittman, a Virginia Republican with no scandals in nearly 20 years in office.

In addition to a stock ban, Taylor wants more punitive sentencing guidelines for lawmakers caught corruptly spending federal dollars and a 12-year limit on serving in each chamber of Congress.

“We’ve got corruption in D.C. that is directly related to why costs keep going up, because politicians are thinking about themselves,” she told The Sun in late September.
Election 2026 Virginia (5944x3963, AR: 1.50)The most radical proposal would be the lifetime ban on leaving Congress for K Street, which is a bipartisan tradition that has gone on for decades.

A 2023 study found that more than 460 former members of Congress were actively employed by lobbying firms. Another study found that last year, 872 former members, ex-staff and other government officials, almost evenly split between Republicans and Democrats, registered to lobby the federal government for the first time, the leading edge of a record number of new lobbyists.

Current laws require a one-year cooling-off period for former House members and two years for ex-senators before they are allowed to lobby their old colleagues on behalf of corporations, associations and other special interests.

Eliminating that revolving door, even if the ban applied only to members and not staff, would be the most significant ethics change on Capitol Hill since the post-Watergate era.

The lobbying community has regularly cited First Amendment rights to petition the government whenever restrictions are imposed, setting up a possible legal battle if the next Congress does impose a wide ban.

“Lobbying is a legitimate and essential part of our democracy. We understand the negative perceptions of our profession that have resulted from some unethical practices by a very few within our profession,” Paul Miller, chair of the National Institute for Lobbying and Ethics, wrote during one such dispute in 2020.

But new majorities can bring in new members who push more aggressively, as was the case with the Democratic majority-making House class of 2018.

“We introduced the idea of the stock trading ban, which at the time, I’ll be honest, congressional leaders were very angry at us. A lot of people opposed it,” Sen. Andy Kim (D-New Jersey) said in an interview with 535 this month.

Kim offered legislation in September 2025 to ban stock trades by congressmen and senior members of the executive and judicial branches, as well as impose a lifetime ban on lawmakers becoming lobbyists. His bill has yet to secure a co-sponsor.

In the House, Rep. Joe Neguse of Colorado led a group of eight Democrats in a series of expansive ethics reforms, including a ban on members serving on corporate boards and tightening bribery rules to make it easier to prosecute members of Congress. Neguse’s legislation to prohibit lawmakers from becoming lobbyists has just seven co-sponsors.

Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii, who will likely become the No. 2 Democratic leader next year, noted that leaders in both parties have forced stock-trading votes but added extraneous, highly partisan proposals, leading to deadlock in the Senate.

Schatz suggested Democrats should offer the stock ban without any other proposals, possibly creating a path for it and other ethics ideas to pass.

“If you want to pass a stock-trading ban, just put the damn thing clean on the floor and it’ll pass both chambers with flying colors,” he told The Sun’s Igor Bobic on a podcast this month.

But that’s just the easy first step. Kim described the stock ban as something that is now a “mainstay which pretty much every candidate has to give their position on” — and Democrats out on the campaign trail are using their ads and rallies to drive up expectations of a much bolder agenda.

In a swing district in northeast Pennsylvania, Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti rolled out a final ad this week that defined her congressional race almost entirely around bold, ethical change that sounds bigger than just a stock ban.

“Here’s what this campaign is about: ending the corruption that hurts our families. Together, we stood up to the machine in Scranton, and together we will take on a corrupt Washington,” she said.

If they don’t take on corruption, Democrats could have a very brief time holding the majority.

entries.title: George Pelecanos Shows Off His D.C. Roots Yet Again
entries.summary: His latest novel is a portrait of the city in 2026 (minus Trump).
entries.content:
George Pelecanos is a neighborhood guy. He is also my neighbor. We live near downtown Silver Spring and frequent the same car mechanic, coffee shop and Vietnamese restaurant. I have never actually run into Pelecanos, the prolific crime novelist and writer and producer on “The Wire,” at any of these establishments, but I was thrilled to see him name-drop all three in “The Blue Flame,” his first D.C.-based novel in 10 years.

This is his 24th work of fiction set in the city, and, like his previous books, it is heavy on specifics as it pays homage to the DMV. Pelecanos was particularly keen on making sure he rendered accurately the site of the book’s climactic scene, a house on Gallatin Street Northeast near 6th Place. To be certain the building could be approached stealthily from an alley in the dark, he cased the place one night.

For Pelecanos, the goal is not just achieving verisimilitude in fiction. It’s about creating a historical record. His D.C. Quartet series — four books published between 1996 and 2000 — took readers from the late 1940s to the 1990s, capturing the ’68 riots, the go-go ’70s and the drug-related poverty of the ’80s and ’90s. In his subsequent novels, Pelecanos has taken readers through the 2000s and into the present with this most recent release. As he explained in a phone interview last month: “When I’m gone, if anybody’s still reading my stories, they can read this book and say, ‘This was what D.C. was like in 2026.’ ”

There is an important caveat: Readers won’t find any mention of President Donald Trump. But Pelecanos has never been interested in that Washington — and he’s never more uninterested than now. He acknowledges Trump’s impact on Washingtonians, but he also thinks residents have been resilient as the president has big-footed D.C. “I feel like they’re tougher than most and they shake it off,” he said. “They go about their lives despite the lies that are told about them and their city.” He added: “I don’t want Trump’s name in any of my books.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Instead, his eye is turned toward the hard workers who aren’t just passing through town because of an election. They are here for the long haul. For this novel, Pelecanos returned to his favorite character: Derek Strange, a detective-turned-PI who has been hired to solve the murder at the center of the book. Strange, Pelecanos explained to me, is someone “I’ve known all of my life, whether in the form of a mentor, or coach, or just the kind of guy I’ve talked to on the street.”

Strange was 12 years old in the 2004 novel “Hard Revolution,” and Pelecanos always intended to tell the full arc of his story. In the latest book, Strange is in his twilight years but has never lost touch with his roots. He keeps an office in Petworth, not far from where he grew up. Though he does much of his detecting from his car and on his feet, Strange, Pelecanos told me, wants to maintain his presence in the neighborhood, so that “young men and women, many moving out of Roosevelt High School on Georgia Avenue, could see a Black man turning the key of his front door, in his own shop, every day.” (Pelecanos, who is white, shakes off those who might criticize him for writing a Black character: “I think if you write the characters well, then it shouldn’t matter.”)

Like Strange, Pelecanos’ roots in D.C. run deep. He was born here, in 1957, and now lives two miles from his childhood home. He spent his early years in Mount Pleasant, living with extended family and working at his father’s diner, the Jefferson Coffee Shop near Dupont Circle. (It was sold in the early ’80s and became the late, lamented C.F. Folks.)

His memories of the diner sound like scenes from his novels: a dishwasher nicknamed Butterball who taught him how to shoot 3-pointers in the alley; a Daily News delivery guy who came in every day at 3 p.m. “to slam a stack of the tabloid newspapers atop the cigarette machine”; his father, Peter, manning the grill, “always at his happiest when he was working his business, what Greeks called the magazi.”

Dupont Circle was a very different place when the Jefferson Coffee Shop opened its doors in the ’60s. It was not lined with boutiques and overpriced restaurants; it was a hotbed of political demonstrations and civil unrest. Delivering food in ’68, just after the riots, was a pivotal moment in Pelecanos’ growth as a person — and as a writer. The author would travel by foot or bus, through corridors where looting and violence had devastated communities. “There was a lot of hardship for people at that time,” he said. But for someone with a bright imagination, it was like “being a kid in England during the war. It was exciting.”

Even after his family moved to Silver Spring, Pelecanos continued to be exhilarated by the city. “I rode the bus downtown to get to work but rode home with my dad after we closed. I looked forward to this ride in his ’68 Dodge Monaco every day,” he told me. “My father’s radio was set on WWDC 1260, and the drive-time DJ was Fred Fiske. The songs by Blood, Sweat and Tears, the Youngbloods and the 5th Dimension were in heavy rotation. My father was quiet, but the quiet was comfortable between us. It was our time.”

Pelecanos is both reverent toward the city’s gritty past and accepting of the metamorphosis that he charts in his series. “I try not to be nostalgic about what it was,” he said. H Street, for example, was one of the last riot corridors that remained burned out and disconnected from the Metro. “If you had gone down there 20 years ago, there was a lot of darkness in those buildings, and now the lights are on,” he said. “What that means is that people have jobs in that neighborhood, and that’s a big deal. I understand concerns about gentrification, but the upside is pretty good.”

Still, the city’s past will always inform Pelecanos’ storytelling. When Strange appeared in the 2004 novel, he was hanging out in an alley demonstrating a three-point stance to his companion, a Greek kid who works at his father’s diner. (Sound familiar?) Now, in “The Blue Flame,” Strange likes to listen to Frankie Beverly and Maze while grilling food for friends in his yard. A true neighborhood guy. Kind of like the Greek kid he befriended in that alley.
