entries.title: The Unlikely Resurgence of Kirsten Gillibrand
entries.summary: An unexpected path to a Senate majority has the junior New York senator (and Chuck Schumer) in line for a political renewal, despite simmering anger on the left.
entries.content:
The prognosis was brutal nearly two years ago when Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand told colleagues and staff that she wanted to run the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm. Reeling from losing their majority in their colossal 2024 losses, even the most optimistic Democrat couldn’t articulate a path back to power in just one cycle.

Now, the junior New York senator and party leaders who have been castigated by their own base for the past two years are unexpectedly tasting the prospect of victory next week.

If Gillibrand and the much-criticized party establishment win a majority in the U.S. Senate that few thought possible so soon, it would leave her and Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, in a politically formidable position.

Gillibrand would even like to run the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for another term, multiple sources familiar with the conversations told The Washington Sun.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read.

Arguing for it, her allies laud her strategic prowess (including candidate recruitment vilified by progressives) and fundraising skills, saying Gillibrand very early on saw the potential for this cycle to parallel the 2006 midterms, an election when Schumer led the DSCC and Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress.

“If she does what I think she’s going to do Tuesday, she’s going to overachieve on a scale we’ve never seen,” one longtime Democratic donor told The Sun. “I think it could outpace 2006, candidly.”

It’s a remarkable spot for the moderate-turned-liberal Democrat who has long had perhaps more than her share of detractors, from those alienated by her role in pushing former Sen. Al Franken to resign in 2017 to more recent critics of her relationship with the cryptocurrency industry. Even her current tenure at the top of the Senate campaign operation has drawn ire from progressives angered by the leaders’ effort to defeat more liberal primary candidates.

Under Gillibrand, the DSCC has raised more than $200 million this election cycle, a haul that committee officials say exceeds its Republican counterpart's fundraising after excluding loans and transfers from national party committees. Earlier this month Gillibrand and the DSCC borrowed $15 million from Amalgamated Bank, according to Federal Election Commission filings, pulling from a revolving line of credit that was increased from $20 million to $25 million this summer.

The fundraising success comes as Democrats have faced broader financial disadvantages beyond the party committees. GOP-aligned outside groups have spent nearly twice as much as the Democrats this cycle. And with limits on coordinated spending between parties and campaigns lifted, the DSCC has faced greater pressure to raise money.

Gillibrand’s allies credit the recruitment of candidates like Ohio’s Sherrod Brown, Alaska’s Mary Peltola and North Carolina’s Roy Cooper for giving the party a path to a majority. Those three candidates, they argue, are uniquely positioned to flip red seats that Democrats critically need. Polling averages from Decision Desk HQ show all three of those Democrats leading the Republican in the race less than a week before election day. And though the DSCC denies it helped recruit a second Dan Sullivan to the Alaska contest to sow confusion, it would be the kind of move insiders hail, as long as the recent unmasking by The New York Times doesn’t make it backfire.

Allies could also point to the competitive primaries in Michigan and Maine, where progressives defeated more moderate candidates who were supported by party leaders. Both are now toss-up contests.

Still, Democratic leaders’ handling of those contested Senate primaries exposed fundamental divisions over the party’s strategy for winning a majority and continues to draw criticism.

Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, a national political group associated with the economic populist wing of the party, argued Gillibrand and Schumer were roadblocks to the push to win back the Senate.

“If Democrats win back control of the Senate it will be in spite of the instincts of Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand,” Green said. “Leaving the garage with your parking brake on — that is Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand.”

That tension remains on display in Michigan, where Schumer and other prominent Democrats endorsed Rep. Haley Stevens over progressive favorite Abdul El-Sayed and where, just this week, Stevens’ fiancé endorsed the Republican in the race, Mike Rogers.

The DSCC and Gillibrand, however, stayed neutral and have worked to repair the rift. The day after El-Sayed’s primary win, Gillibrand called him to offer her and the DSCC’s full support, according to a source familiar with that conversation. She also urged Democratic colleagues to push money to El-Sayed’s campaign down the home stretch of the Michigan campaign. Schumer and a major super PAC aligned with the Democratic leader also started supporting El-Sayed the day after his win.

The longtime Democratic donor insists the DSCC brass didn’t try to sway the race in Michigan.

“They weren’t asking reliable donors to weigh in on the primary,” the donor said. “I’ve seen other races where they’ve tried to push money. I’m one of the first phone calls they would make. I never got that call.”

The griping isn’t confined to progressive strategists. Some Democratic senators have publicly and privately questioned the DSCC’s involvement in divisive primaries. That included its support of former Maine Gov. Janet Mills, who was recruited by Schumer but ended her campaign in the face of a surge by Graham Platner, the left’s darling who later dropped out amid allegations of sexual assault. The committee spent considerable resources supporting Mills and helped her raise money.

Supporters of Democratic leadership counter the critics by pointing to the more moderate candidates recruited by leadership who are out-performing progressives in polls in key races.

“To suggest Democratic leadership has been ineffective when we’re on the verge of taking back a Senate majority that almost nobody thought was within reach a year ago is the height of absurdity,” said a senior Democrat with knowledge of the races.

“Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand has been instrumental in our efforts to expand the Senate map, run strong campaigns, and ensure Democrats and the DSCC have the resources needed to compete and win,” a spokesperson for the DSCC said in a statement. “The battle for a Senate majority is now a toss-up and Democrats have never been better positioned than they are today, thanks in large part to the work of Chair Gillibrand.”

Even critics admit a strong result next week would bolster Gillibrand’s case to run the DSCC again. The demands of the job are such that many senators don’t find it desirable, and the gig is primarily a fundraising job, with a significant travel schedule and time spent dealing with donors, campaigns and candidates.

“She sucks but I don’t think there’s anyone else willing,” one senior Democratic aide said. “And if we take back the Senate, she and Schumer will take credit.”

Gillibrand also has a unique trait that comes into play running the DSCC — she’s extremely familiar with Schumer, who maintains a strong interest in its operations. The focus on campaigns remains central to Schumer’s political identity, and the Democratic leader takes the lion’s share of credit (and blame) for his caucus’ electoral success.

Sources around both lawmakers said Gillibrand has learned to manage that dynamic with Schumer over years of working together representing New York. The sources said the junior New York Democrat doesn’t step on Schumer’s toes in her DSCC job and knows what is likely to get under his skin. The arrangement also works, the sources argued, because Gillibrand isn’t ego-driven in the role.

Allison Biasotti, a spokesperson for Schumer, praised Gillibrand’s partnership with the Democratic leader.

“As we’ve expanded the map, raised record amounts of money, and put Democrats within striking distance of taking back the Senate — something few thought possible a year ago — Senator Gillibrand has been an outstanding partner to Leader Schumer,” Biasotti said in a statement.

While some senators see the campaign chief job as thankless, some, including Schumer himself, have used it as a launch pad. As Gillibrand seeks another term leading the DSCC, a victory next week, especially one of historic proportions, strengthens her case.

The longtime Democratic donor said if Senate Democrats win next week, the question won’t be whether Gillibrand is asked to run the committee again, but “whether she will accept the offer from her caucus.”

entries.title: What Should We Expect From AJ Dybantsa? Former No. 1 Picks Weigh In.
entries.summary: The Wizards’ top overall pick made his NBA debut this week.
entries.content:
AJ Dybantsa was two questions into his first media day as an NBA player when a Howard University student asked the question.

Does Dybantsa feel any pressure as the Wizards’ first No. 1 overall pick since John Wall 16 years ago?

“None,” Dybantsa answered.

“Really?” the reporter replied.

“Yeah,” Dybantsa said. “I’m all good.”

The 19-year-old, whose professional debut was delayed by an ankle injury he suffered during the preseason, is one of the most highly touted prospects in recent years. But he is entering a situation with Washington that’s different from the one faced by many players at his draft slot — he’s joining a team that’s ready to win right away, with a pair of veteran stars in Trae Young and Anthony Davis.

“I feel like there’s not a lot of pressure on me because I have such a great team around me,” said Dybantsa, who referred to the fact that he might not have a big enough role this season to earn Rookie of the Year honors a “blessing in disguise.”

“A lot of No. 1 picks come into a situation where they are the guy, everything is kind of set up around them,” he added. “But I have All-Stars on my team that I can really get under and get some knowledge from. So I don’t have to come in and carry this huge load.”

What can Dybantsa expect as he begins his career? We spoke with several former first overall picks to get their insights.

John Wall

The last player to be selected first overall for the Wizards, Wall, who took four years to reach the playoffs, was tasked with being the franchise’s savior right away. He said Dybantsa getting to share the load with the Wizards’ veterans should work to his advantage.

“It’s great for him because there’s not too much pressure on him,” Wall told The Washington Sun. “He doesn’t have to come in and be the guy right away. I mean, yeah, he’s the future of what it’s gonna be, but to have [Davis and Young], he can lean on them for a lot of things. He can fill in the void and expand his game. Most times, you come in, they put the ball in your hands and run plays through you. Now he can be a backseat guy and sit in the corner and be the slasher, then have the ball in pick-and-rolls.”

Anthony Davis

Davis entered into a similar situation as Wall, tasked with turning around a New Orleans franchise that had struggled. It wasn’t until his third year, Davis said, when the team added the All-Star veteran Rajon Rondo, that the Pelicans’ culture and ability to compete changed.

Now, Dybantsa has that in Davis as a rookie instead of having to wait for it.

“I say it to the guys all the time,” Davis said at media day. “I’ve been here before. Where the team isn't good and you get a couple pieces and you’re now looked at a team who can do something.”

Unlike Davis, Dybantsa will have that experience right away. He also has many of the tools he’ll need to succeed early, said Davis, who helped mentor another No. 1 overall pick last season for the Dallas Mavericks in then-rookie Cooper Flagg.

“I think the ones that are special, like [Flagg] and obviously AJ, they want it,” Davis said. “They want to learn, they want to get better, they ask questions, the right questions. I’ve been able to give AJ a little bit about how it’s going to be coming into the league. He’s going to have a target on his back, everyone’s going to want to come after him. Same thing I was doing with Coop last year. He’s ready for it. He’s got all the tools to be successful in this league.”

After Dybantsa’s NBA debut on Wednesday, the rookie said he "definitely had some butterflies.” Davis said he couldn’t relate to Dybantsa’s nerves because his own career had a unique start.

“My path was also different,” Davis told reporters. “I didn’t play Summer League. I was with the [2012 London] Olympics. So by the time I got into my first game, I played for 2 months with the Hall of Famers, so the nerves were kind of [not] there. I felt like I belonged already.”

Blake Griffin

Some top picks say the pressure that comes with the selection is overthought. Blake Griffin, who went No. 1 overall in 2009, said external expectations weren’t on his mind during his own career.

“When I was playing, you didn’t feel the pressure of being a No. 1 pick,” Griffin told The Sun. “You just want to be good. As a player, that’s your main focus is getting better and producing.”

Deandre Ayton

But that doesn’t mean his situation remains unenvious despite an unknown outcome. Ayton, who went No. 1 in 2018 to the Suns said Dybantsa is “very lucky and blessed” to be drafted by a team with a locker room of veterans and teammates who have been in his shoes. It’s why Ayton is bullish on how it’s going to work out for him.

“He’s really protected and he gets to really be who AJ is,” Ayton said. “It’s going to be hard for him to fail, really. ”

entries.title: Thune Says Republicans Have 'Done All We Can Do' Before the Midterms
entries.summary: The Senate majority leader defended his party’s record heading into Election Day, but admits “headwinds” shifted the map.
entries.content:
CLYDE, Ohio — Senate Majority Leader John Thune says he has few regrets about his party’s record and is already waving off fellow Republicans stirring up a blame game about the midterm elections.

Senate Republicans could be days away from losing their majority, with the party needing to suddenly shift big money to red states they believed should have been safe seats.

But on the trail in what has traditionally been a solidly red state, the Republican leader isn’t ready for any Monday morning quarterbacking about what his party could have done differently.

“It's a broader map,” Thune says from the kitchen table of a northern Ohio home. “We've done all we can do, and with the things that we can control.”

When pressed on what’s keeping him up at night, Thune points to the Republican firewall states of Maine, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska. Beyond that, he namechecks Texas, Kansas and Nebraska before acknowledging what he calls “the tough political environment.”

“The president’s not on the ballot, so there's some headwinds that our candidates are dealing with, but they're really high-quality candidates.”

GOP candidates have found themselves on the back foot after months of being battered by the Iran war, and gas and food prices that have remained stubbornly high ever since the conflict began. They’re also dragged down by President Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings that aren’t doing his members much good.

Thune immediately pointed to Sen. Jon Husted, the Republican who is running against former Sen. Sherrod Brown for his first full term and whom Thune is on the road to boost. He's been joined by other prominent Republicans including Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz.
20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_2219.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_1641.jpg (7658x5108, AR: 1.50)Husted, however, is having trouble getting over the hump. Polls show that he and Brown are in a nip-and-tuck race. One unclear factor is whether Vivek Ramaswamy, the party’s candidate for Ohio governor, will drag him down. Ramaswamy’s campaign started cratering after his decision to air a controversial ad featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent who was allegedly sexually abused by her stepfather when she was 12 years old.

Multiple Republicans, including Husted, have argued that the ad was a mistake or that it should be pulled down. Thune indicated that Husted is in the right here.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read.

“I think … there's been enough spent defining candidates in both the governor's race and the Senate races here that I think people are going to be able to differentiate,” Thune said. “I feel really good about our chances here.”

Ohio was among the final stops on the trail for the leader, who campaigned in nearly a dozen places in recent weeks, including in Iowa late last week for Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Senate nominee in another battleground race.

The South Dakota Republican’s lack of second-guessing also applies to the Senate GOP’s response to the unpopular Iran war, which has sent fuel prices soaring. In Ohio, gas prices average $4.26 per gallon, with diesel costs nearing $6.50 per gallon on average.

Thune has sung a consistent tune since the war kicked off in February: that the war should wrap up sooner rather than later, that the Strait of Hormuz should be open and that once the war concludes, prices will normalize. It’s taken longer than he imagined, but he defends his party sticking behind the Trump administration’s strategy.

“I don't think we were in a position, frankly, that we could have done anything differently. As I look back on the last year … in the category of things that we can control, I think we did everything we possibly could,” Thune said. “When you're in a situation like that, where you've got troops deployed in harm's way, everybody kind of surrounds the flag and makes sure that we stick together for the country.  Now, I'm hopeful that the president and his team will bring this to a fairly quick end. I feel like we're getting there.”

Whether that happens remains to be seen. The White House has indicated to allies in the Middle East that a “short, intense military campaign” against Iran is expected once the midterms conclude, according to The Wall Street Journal.

As for his own political future, Thune is expected to run for a second term leading the Republican conference, despite some discontent among members on his right flank.
20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_2699.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)There are a number of questions in the leadership race, including whether Trump will get involved one way or another. Thune recently told CBS News that he isn’t banking on Trump’s support.

Helping Thune out is that there is no obvious challenger at this point.

“[Thune] doesn’t hire senators. He doesn’t fire senators. He doesn’t set our pay. He can’t reprimand us. Other than that, he’s the leader,” Ohio’s other Republican senator, Bernie Moreno, told The Sun with a laugh during an interview. “It’s a thankless job. He does a great job.”

“He’s an incredible human being. Probably too nice sometimes,” Moreno said. “But look, he’s going to be the leader of the conference one way or the other. Nobody’s running against him, and I think that’s the way it should be.”

But Thune has found himself on the wrong side of some of Trump’s MAGA allies and his own colleagues who demanded he pass the SAVE America Act, the hardline voting bill that has no avenue of passage in the upper chamber.

Some of those backers are already laying the groundwork to blame the Senate Republican leader if the midterms go south for the party. Unsurprisingly, Thune is used to the constant criticism.

“They blame me for everything,” he said. “You got people out there … they're going to complain when their ice cream's cold. There's just a lot of people who are never gonna be happy.”

On top of an already-brewing blame game, Thune is also preparing for what could be an onerous lame duck session, especially if Republicans lose the chamber. Leading the to-do list is funding the government, a defense authorization bill and farmer’s assistance legislation. He is also eyeing a permitting reform bill that is set to be the first item to hit the floor during the two-month work session, pending Democratic cooperation.

The big “if” remains whether a third budget reconciliation package is on the agenda, especially if this marks the final weeks of the Republican trifecta. Moreno recently told reporters that losing control in Congress would prompt a “last supper” vehicle for the party to cram in priorities of all stripes, but it’s unclear what could pass.

“Right now, we don't have the votes to get on a third recon bill [and a] budget resolution. … We might have them after [the midterms],” Thune said. “We don’t have it now, and we don’t know that we have the votes to defend against the poison pill Democrat amendments.”
20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_5032.jpg (8145x5433, AR: 1.50)20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_5132.jpg (8136x5427, AR: 1.50)He said there are unknown factors: “The question is, how does the election outcome change that? I think the election outcome obviously is probably going to shape in a very significant way what's achievable in the lame duck.” He also admitted, “it's going to be the art of the doable.”

While talk in the immediate term focuses on his future as leader, questions have also risen about how long Thune plans to stick around the Capitol.

He took a full year to decide whether to run for a fourth term in 2022. But he has already indicated that he will seek a fifth term in 2028, with an official announcement likely to come sooner rather than later.

“We'll start putting the wheels in motion fairly quickly on that,” he said about a timeline for a decision. Referring to his critics on the right, he said, “obviously, there's all this speculation that they'll come after me and want to primary me. They did that last time.”

“I'm fully confident that we can survive both primary and general elections, but it's got to be the right thing to do,” Thune continued. “That's always a conversation my wife and I have — kind of about where we are in life, and where we think we can make the biggest difference, and I feel like the job I have right now is a bit of a calling.”

entries.title: Unexpected Air Force One Flyover Gives Washington a Halloween Fright
entries.summary: “It startled many, including us,” the D.C. Council posted on social media.
entries.content:
A low-altitude Air Force One flyover during President Donald Trump’s White House Halloween celebration Thursday drew condemnation from officials and residents, with the D.C. Council saying it received only 15 minutes’ notice before the plane flew over downtown Washington.

In a tweet posted on Thursday, the council said local officials, the Pentagon and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport were not provided ample notice before the display.

“It startled many, including us,” the council members wrote.

An alert pushed out by Washington, D.C., on Thursday at 5:23 p.m. stated: “The U.S. Military will conduct an Aircraft Flyover in the NCR over the National Mall area today over the next hour.”

The flyover occurred as the president and first lady Melania Trump passed out candy at the White House on Thursday, an annual presidential tradition.

The Washington Sun has emailed the White House for comment.
https://x.com/councilofdc/status/2115971837624459340The Federal Aviation Administration said the flyover was coordinated with the agency in an emailed statement to The Washington Sun.

Several D.C. residents took issue with how low the aircraft flew, stating they were nervous about a pending attack. According to public flight tracking data, the plane flew as low as 375 feet at one point.

“I saw this while driving south on 13th St NW in DC this evening,” posted Larry Pfeiffer, executive director of the Hayden Center for Intelligence, Policy and International Security.

“I didn't recognize it as AF1, as it flew by so quickly. I couldn't imagine why a plane would fly so low over the city, near the White House, and I was waiting to hear a ‘boom,’” he added. “Too many years fighting terrorists.”

Daniel Fried, another D.C. resident, said: “I’m one of those Washingtonians who saw the low-flying plane and wondered whether it was a terrorist attack or a plane about to crash. Glad it was neither but not a funny stunt.”

According to FlightAware data, 203 flights were delayed at Reagan National Airport on Thursday, with many caused by a brief ground stop from the flyover.

The plane, a new $400 million Boeing 747-8, was gifted to the president by Qatar. Trump took his inaugural flight on the retrofitted plane in July.

The last time a 747 flew at such a low altitude in Washington, D.C., was in 2012, when a Space Shuttle Discovery flew over the city on the back of a plane.

entries.title: Trump Resurrects Canceled Rallies in Iowa and Kansas
entries.summary: A source familiar with the situation told The Washington Sun that the rallies were “rearranged for scheduling purposes.”
entries.content:
President Donald Trump will attend midterm rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday, resurrecting the events just hours after the White House announced it was canceling them.

“President Trump loves his supporters, and in addition to nearly 20 tele-rallies, he will hold back-to-back rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday,” a source familiar with the situation told The Washington Sun, saying that the rallies were “rearranged for scheduling purposes” so that the president could attend more tele-rallies over the weekend.

“No one works harder, fights harder, or loves the American people more than President Donald J. Trump!” the source said.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

entries.title: Pope Leo XIV Is the First Pope in History to Vote in a U.S. General Election
entries.summary: The Vatican said the pope submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago.
entries.content:
VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election, casting a mail-in ballot in a contest that will decide America's future as the Trump era slowly comes to an end.

The Vatican confirmed Friday that the Chicago-born pontiff had submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, citing his long-standing belief in civic participation.

Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen” and has done so “whenever he was eligible to do so,” the Holy See press office said.

The statement said he had also voted while living in Peru whenever he was eligible. Leo lived in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop for over 20 years.

“The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” it added.

Leo holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship, and is also the head of state of a foreign country, the Holy See. The city state is an absolute monarchy with no political elections.

This election, Illinois voters are deciding whether to elect Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to his third term, and they’re also filling an open U.S. Senate seat after longtime Catholic Democrat Dick Durbin’s retirement. President Donald Trump is not on the ballot but he has campaigned hard to try to preserve Republican control of the U.S. House and Senate for the final two years of his second term.

Leo’s vote was first reported by the Chicago Sun-Times, which quoted the chief of staff at the Will County clerk’s office as saying the pope, registered at a New Lenox address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3.

The request was made just 10 days before Leo underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Leo has been slowly resuming his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital Oct. 17.

It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. The pope's older brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St. Jude’s, an Augustinian-run parish in New Lenox, Illinois. The elder Prevost attends Mass there, and Leo gave a talk at the parish in 2024 while still a cardinal.

Prevost's Past Votes Have Gone Democratic and Republican

Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections.

The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a primary ballot. No such declaration is required in general elections.

While registered in heavily Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative suburban Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.

The records also show that he submitted ballots in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022.

Clashes with Trump

Since becoming pope, Leo has drawn criticism from President Donald Trump for repeatedly condemning the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran and calling for dignified treatment of immigrants.

Earlier this year, Trump called Leo “weak” and captive to the “radical left.”

Responding to Trump’s public rebuke, Leo told reporters en route to Algeria in April: “I’m not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the church works for.”

“I will continue to speak out strongly against war, seeking to promote peace, promoting dialogue and multilateralism among states to find solutions to problems,” he said.

The public dispute has subsided in recent months.

The Pope Follows U.S. Politics Closely

Leo has made clear on several occasions that he follows local and national U.S. politics closely, and is not afraid to intervene.

He has repeatedly called for reflection and humane treatment for immigrants in his native U.S. amid the Trump administration crackdown and mass deportation program.

Recently, Leo reiterated official church teaching declaring the death penalty “inadmissible.” He made the pronouncement in a social media post on the World Day Against the Death Penalty, which came as the U.S. announced plans to livestream an execution by firing squad. The plans were later scrapped.

In 2025, Leo intervened in a debate over abortion, after Chicago Cardinal Blase Cupich announced plans to give a lifetime achievement award to Sen. Durbin. The plans drew objection from some conservative U.S. bishops given the powerful Democratic senator’s support for abortion rights. Leo called for respect for both sides, but he also pointed out the contradiction between people who call themselves “pro-life” but also support the death penalty.

Also in 2025, Leo said he was “very disappointed” that his home state of Illinois approved a law allowing medically assisted dying, which is condemned by the Catholic Church.

AP editor Holly Meyer contributed from Nashville, Tenn.

entries.title: A Colorado Congressional Candidate Has a ‘Principal Residence’ in Maryland
entries.summary: Democrat Jessica Killin is running against Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a tight race.
entries.content:
Jessica Killin, the Democratic candidate for Colorado’s 5th Congressional District, has a “principal residence” in Maryland, according to Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation records reviewed by The Washington Sun.

A Maryland property tax bill due Oct. 31 lists a house in Chevy Chase, Maryland, as being owned by Killin and her husband, Rajeev Date, and having a tax balance of $14,306 due. The assessed value of the home is $2.33 million, according to the document.

After The Sun asked Killin’s campaign about the property records, Killin filed paperwork on Oct. 27 with the Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation to change her mailing address from the Chevy Chase home just north of Washington, D.C., to one in Colorado Springs, Colorado.

Emily Dalgleish, Killin’s campaign manager, told The Sun, “Jessica Killin is a Colorado resident. The paperwork was outdated. It’s been updated and resolved.”

As of Friday, Maryland property records list Killin’s Chevy Chase house as her “principal residence” and her Colorado Springs house as her mailing address. The Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation says it takes three to four days for an address to be updated within the system after filing.

In an email to The Sun, Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation spokesperson Alyssa Nolte said that “a principal residence is the property where the owner lives for the majority of the year, which is at least 6 months and 1 day.”

Nolte added that second homes should not be considered principal residences, though “certain situations may be approved on a case-by-case basis.”

Even though Killin grew up in Colorado Springs, her address has been subject to scrutiny from her Republican opponent, Rep. Jeff Crank.

“She air-dropped in, in June of last year. Prior to that, she lived in Maryland. She lived in a mansion in Maryland until June,” Crank said in August, according to the Colorado Times Recorder.

Nick Trainer, a Crank campaign adviser, told The Sun that Killin’s Colorado home is a “campaign prop” and said Killin “thought she could pull off the gambit with the people of El Paso County” in Colorado. Trainer did not respond to other questions about Killin’s property records.

Crank accused Killin of registering to vote in Colorado and run for Congress “a few days” after she and her husband purchased a $3.5 million home in Colorado’s El Paso County in June 2025.
Jeff.Crank.1 (8256x5504, AR: 1.50)Killin’s statement of candidacy filed with the Federal Election Commission is dated July 15, 2025. The Killin campaign provided The Sun documentation indicating Killin registered to vote in Colorado on July 10, 2025.

Killin had a two-decade-long career in Washington where she worked as a Democratic congressional aide, assistant vice president of federal government relations for insurer USAA and as the former chief of staff for former second gentleman Doug Emhoff, the husband of Kamala Harris, before purchasing the Colorado home and deciding to run to represent Colorado.

Killin has listed both her Maryland and Colorado addresses when making recent political contributions to Democratic candidates and the Colorado Democratic Party in 2025 and 2026.

A donation made in August 2025 to the political committee Electing Women Denver identifies Killin as a Colorado congressional candidate with an address in Chevy Chase.

The Cook Political Report rated Colorado’s 5th Congressional District as a “toss up” Friday morning, a shift from its previous “lean Republican” rating.

entries.title: ICE Officer Has Been Charged After Striking a Man With a Car in Houston
entries.summary: The Harris County District Attorney's office charged the officer with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.
entries.content:
By Anna Wilder and Lekan Oyekanmi

HOUSTON — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston was charged Friday with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, prosecutors said.

The Harris County District Attorney's office says Mario Alberto Morales was behind the wheel of an unmarked black vehicle on Oct. 10 when it struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, who was running away. Parra Hernandez was later placed in custody with a broken leg.

Few federal officers during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown have faced criminal charges for their actions in the field, although some encounters have come under investigation.

The case in Houston was brought by District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, who is also investigating the fatal shooting of a Mexican homebuilder in July that set off protests in the nation’s fourth-largest city.

ICE did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment about the indictment charging Morales.

ICE has said Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the car and called accusations that the officer intentionally struck him false and “reckless.” Teare has said the surveillance footage clearly contradicts the ICE account.

In the video, a Jeep Cherokee speeds over a median and drives toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away. The video does not show the car hitting him — that view is blocked by another vehicle — but it shows the SUV inches away from him. The footage then shows Parra Hernandez on the ground.

Family Says ICE Was Looking for a Dead Person During the Operation

Other aspects of ICE's account have also been called into question.

ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day and was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him. FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston, said Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017. She also said his real name is Jose Hector Jimenez.

Teare's office has also said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE's statement.

ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for nearly a decade.

Parra Hernandez has been in the country for more than 30 years. He was living in the U.S. without authorization, according to FIEL, which has been working with his family.

Fatal Summer Houston Shooting Also Under Investigation

Teare said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence “either intentionally or through gross negligence.” He said the ICE officer who drove the SUV that struck Parra Hernandez fled the scene before the vehicle could be impounded.

In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his requests for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his van. DHS has said Salgado Araujo had “weaponized his vehicle” before the shooting and that an officer fired in self-defense. Other passengers in the van have disputed that account.

Teare has not given a timetable for when his office's investigation into the shooting will be complete. In September, a witness to the shooting was seen entering a courthouse area reserved for grand jury proceedings.

Wilder reported from Austin.

entries.title: Appeals Court Again Denies DOJ’s California Noncitizen Ballot Push
entries.summary: The state told judges that segregating 20,000 ballots of potential noncitizen voters would completely change its procedures.
entries.content:
An appeals court again rejected a Trump administration request to stop California from counting the votes of over 20,000 people the government identified as potential noncitizen voters.

The Justice Department had asked the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to force California to sequester the ballots and establish a process to verify the citizenship status of those voters before counting them.

In a 2-1 order, the court ruled the DOJ’s emergency request is not as easy as the government purports.

“The United States’s requested relief is simple only in the abstract,” the order says. “As the district court found—and we discern no clear error—there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system.”

The order also stated that California has the constitutional power to administer its own elections and that state law already prohibits noncitizen voting. To conduct a full audit on the state’s millions of mail-in ballots, based on a list of suspected noncitizens, is not feasible with the time left before election night, the order says.

The DOJ sued California earlier this month after the government gave a letter and a thumb drive listing 20,000 people the DOJ believed could be noncitizens who automatically received a mail-in ballot.

The state’s refusal to comply with the DOJ’s request spiraled quickly into a case that is challenging the Trump administration’s last-ditch efforts to control election administration.

A federal judge ruled Thursday that the government’s request to segregate a tranche of ballots was delivered too late in the elections process and that its attempts to isolate noncitizen voters lacked credibility, potentially leading to erroneously disenfranchised voters.

In previous arguments before the court, California told judges that segregating ballots would completely change the state’s procedure, likely forcing it to sort out potential noncitizen ballots by hand.

entries.title: Alaska's Senate Results Could Be Excruciatingly Slow
entries.summary: The state’s expected slow ballot count in the pivotal U.S. Senate race could make Alaska a flashpoint for post-election disputes.
entries.content:
There’s a scenario where the balance of power in the Senate hinges on whether Democrat Mary Peltola or Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan won a close Alaska Senate race. If that happens, the country could find itself waiting.

And waiting. And waiting.

Alaska election officials will have 15 days to count ballots after Election Day because the state accepts absentee ballots later than most: They can be postmarked, rather than received, by Election Day. Normally, though, all of Washington isn’t as absorbed in the results of the far-off state as they have been during this midterm season.

President Donald Trump is questioning the integrity of the race. The Justice Department is suing election officials over a candidate with the same name as the Republican incumbent. And the Republican governor of the state has ordered an investigation after The New York Times published a report on an effort by Democrats to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan, the other Sullivan on the ballot, to run for office to siphon votes away from the incumbent Sullivan. 

Election experts worry that a lag in results could allow time for conspiracies to spread, and they’re preaching patience.

“Election officials during that time are going to roll up their sleeves and continue just doing their jobs and report the election results out,” said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonprofit that supports fair elections. “It is going to take a long time to know who won every race, and it may take days to know who controls Congress.”

Alaska election officials plan to certify the results by Nov. 25 — after that, the results go to Alaska’s governor for certification (another problem this year: Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has not committed to certifying the result. His successor — potentially a Democrat — is due to be sworn in on Dec. 7).

The Alaska Division of Elections did not respond to a request for comment.

There’s also another quirk to voting in the state that makes it different from how voting in much of the rest of the country works: ranked-choice voting.

Voters in Alaska will rank the four Senate candidates who advanced from the nonpartisan open primary in order of preference. If no candidate receives more than 50% of first-choice votes in the initial round of counting, officials proceed to additional rounds of tabulation. Last-place candidates are eliminated, and the ballots roll over to the voter’s next-preferred candidates until a candidate wins a majority.

Alaskans narrowly approved the ranked-choice voting system through a ballot measure in 2020, though opponents of the system criticized the fact that much of the spending in support of that measure came from out of state.

Scott Kendall, who wrote and litigated the 2020 ballot measure, said it’s a common misconception that Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system is to blame for slow ballot counting. Kendall said the reason why tabulation is so slow is because of Alaska’s late deadline to accept absentee ballots and the state’s sheer size.

“The elections are no more delayed than they would be otherwise,” Kendall said.

“You have to analyze each ballot envelope, make sure it's a registered voter, make sure they didn't vote before, check it again,” Kendall said. “It just takes days and days and days.”

There’s an initiative to get rid of the ranked-choice voting system in Alaska on this year’s ballot, with supporters accusing the system of being too complicated. Vice President JD Vance, while leaving a rally on Oct. 29, called ranked-choice voting “confusing.”

“The person who wins the most votes should win,” Vance said. “That seems to be not what happens with ranked-choice voting.”

Kendall, who has worked for Alaska Republicans in the past, said the system mitigates “dirty tricks” because of the roll over to the voter’s next-preferred candidates.

“Sit back, be patient, give the division workers grace because they are overworked, and do not entertain goofy-ass conspiracy theory stuff,” Kendall said. “Just let the results be the results.”

In 2024, the tabulation of votes wasn’t available until Nov. 20, 2024, 15 days after Election Day. The majority of other states require absentee ballots to arrive by Election Day.

Kendall also warned there may be a “partisan skew” to ballots counted later in the process because most of them are mailed in and added that “that doesn't mean it's anything illegitimate. It just means those ballots have been received.”

According to an analysis from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Election Lab, 37% of Democrats voted by mail in 2024 compared to 24% of Republicans. The partisan skew was even more dramatic in 2020: 60% of Democrats compared 32% of Republicans. This year, as trust in the U.S. Postal Service to deliver ballots on time has dropped, there’s reason to believe that Democrats might rely on vote-by-mail less than in the past — but in a state as vast as Alaska, some have no choice.

While most voters cast their ballots in person, 1 in 7 Alaskans vote by mail, according to U.S. Election Assistance Commission data, especially in more remote areas.

In California, where there are often delays in counting votes because most residents mail in their ballots, election deniers have raised doubt during waiting periods before. That happened in several counties across the state in the aftermath of the 2020 election.

“Lengthy delays in final vote tallies, especially in those, you know, where it matters … where the vote margin is very low, it definitely contributes to doubt,” said Cathy Darling Allen, a Democrat and former election official in Shasta County, California. “It only allows election deniers to amplify … that kind of message.”

She added: “There's never going to be a time when a local election official has a bigger microphone than the president of the United States.”

entries.title: The Trump Administration Is Buoying Nearly Half of All U.S. Coal Plants
entries.summary: Between taxpayer-funded payments, regulation exemptions and mandates to remain open, the government has ramped up its support for coal.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is providing support for nearly half of all coal plants connected to the electric grid, according to a new analysis from environmental advocacy nonprofit Environmental Defense Fund.

That federal support comes in the form of taxpayer-funded payments, exemptions from pollution regulations and mandates for certain plants to continue running past their retirement dates — all actions the Trump administration has taken over the last two years to buoy an industry that has been in decline for more than a decade.

As of this summer, 90 of the country’s 184 grid-connected coal plants have received some kind of federal assistance, the Environmental Defense Fund found. Under the Biden administration, federal support for the industry mostly consisted of tax credits for carbon capture and money to help communities transitioning away from coal.

Since early 2025, the Trump administration has reversed course. Seventy coal plants have been granted Clean Air Act exemptions that allow them to get around the 2024 Mercury and Air Toxics Standards. Hundreds of millions in public dollars — some of which was originally appropriated for carbon-capture programs — are going to 24 plants, including two projects to build new coal-fired units in Alaska and West Virginia. And six plants have been ordered to continue operating past their retirement dates, which the Environmental Defense Fund says has “already added hundreds of millions of dollars to families’ electric bills.”

The group’s analysis shows just how quickly the Trump administration has moved to support coal — a push that comes as that industry scrambles to stem its downturn. Despite the federal support, coal continues to become a smaller part of the U.S. electric grid.

The administration’s actions are in line with what the coal industry has asked for. Michelle Bloodworth, president and CEO of America’s Power, a trade association representing coal plants, wrote to Energy Secretary Chris Wright in March 2025 suggesting many of the actions the Trump administration eventually announced. She floated using emergency orders to keep coal units operating for longer, asked for economic support for coal-fired generators and said repealing Environmental Protection Agency regulations could help keep plants online.

Bloodworth also suggested using the Defense Production Act to “preserve the coal supply chain.” Roughly a year later, President Donald Trump issued an executive order to that effect.

Wright has framed the administration’s support for coal as a necessary step to keep the grid reliable.

“Forcing reliable, dispatchable coal generation off the grid would compromise energy reliability and needlessly raises energy costs for Americans,”  Wright said in a statement in September after issuing emergency orders to keep two coal plants in Indiana online.

Burning coal has gotten more expensive. The Environmental Defense Fund’s analysis found it was 28% more expensive to generate power using coal in 2024 than it was in 2021.

“They are propping up the coal industry precisely because it is not economically competitive,” said Seth Feaster, an energy data analyst at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis.

Even utilities are skittish about continuing to use coal, he said, as the plants, many of which were built in the 1950s, become increasingly obsolete.

Gas plants are more efficient, take less people to run and can turn on and off faster to balance the needs of the power grid — a key aspect of reliability, especially as renewable energy becomes a bigger part of the mix. Many gas plants can get up and running within an hour, while most coal plants take half a day to boot up.

Renewables, too, are getting cheaper. The Environmental Defense Fund’s analysis found that almost every coal plant in the U.S. was more expensive to run in 2021 than to replace with wind or solar.

Coal plant owners themselves have balked at the idea of keeping old, expiring facilities online. Electric utilities that own a coal-fired unit in Colorado asked the Energy Department to reconsider a mandate to keep the facility open after a mechanical failure.

The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals last month shot down the Trump administration’s effort to force a Michigan coal plant to stay online past retirement, but the administration has continued reissuing orders for other plants.

Several of the coal plants that are being kept online by orders from the Energy Department aren’t actually generating power. But keeping those plants online is still costing power customers money, Feaster said.

“That bill hasn’t come in yet, but it’s going to be very expensive,” he said. Even more so if plants are forced to do major repairs to remain open.

Despite its wide reach, the Trump administration’s efforts to prop up coal plants may not have lasting impact. As 2028 draws closer and the marketplace moves further from coal, Feaster said he anticipates more utilities will request retirement dates for their plants.

“The moment that it looks like those kinds of policies are gone, you will see a whole bunch of coal plants retire officially because they’re not economically competitive,” he said.

entries.title: Texas Supreme Court Halts Deposition Over Trans-Care Mailers Sent From Unknown Sources
entries.summary: Ongoing litigation concerns revelations about pamphlets allegedly sent out by the Republican Women’s Caucus Fund, not the Transgender Education Network of Texas.
entries.content:
The Texas Supreme Court on Friday halted proceedings that could have offered insight into an election-season campaign referencing gender-affirming care for minors, which has roiled voters in the weeks before Election Day, as more questions arise as to the messages’ origins.

Earlier this month, Texas voters received text messages and mailers advertising gender-affirming care for minors and instructions on how to seek legal emancipation from unsupportive parents. The messaging identified a Texas LGBTQ+ student union as the sender.

But in a deposition given Thursday, the messaging company Infobip stated that the text messages were commissioned by the “Republican Women’s Caucus Fund” — which denied it was involved — and an individual named John Braun. The Texas Observer was the first to report the group’s alleged ties to the mailers.

The Transgender Education Network of Texas — the nonprofit that is repeatedly referenced on the pamphlets — petitioned a Travis County judge to make the true source public. The trans rights organization said that it was not involved in the pamphlets' creation and that it has received threats as a result of the campaign.

A judge in Texas, Jan Soifer, ruled Wednesday that the organization has suffered injuries such as harassment and a diversion of resources as a result of being named in the mailers.

According to the Texas district court docket, TENT appealed the case Tuesday, and asked Soifer to remove a confidential information designation from Infobip’s answers during the deposition on Thursday, which she granted that day.

The state Supreme Court on Friday paused a deposition scheduled for later that morning that would have revealed more information about who sent out the pamphlets and text messages. The court issued a deadline of Monday for initial responses, noting in its order that TENT’s motion for relief is still pending.

No court documents were available online at the district, appeals or state Supreme Court levels as of Friday afternoon.

The pamphlets claimed to have been sent by the Texas Transgender Student Union — a group that was registered as a limited liability company in Wyoming one month ago, an Observer investigation found.

A Republican Women’s Caucus Fund spokesperson denied being involved.

“We did not authorize, fund, direct, coordinate, or participate in these activities in any capacity,” the spokesperson told The Texas Tribune on Thursday. “We categorically reject these false allegations and are pursuing all available legal remedies to protect our organization and hold those responsible accountable.”

Vice President JD Vance was asked about the campaign during a town hall in Weatherford, Texas, on Thursday. One woman described finding a pamphlet in her mail addressed to her young daughter that offered detailed instructions on how to transition genders.

The person who sent the letter is “a pervert,” Vance told the woman, and “ought to go to prison.”

“Talk to our staff because I’d like the Department of Justice to investigate that,” he said.

The campaign has caused outrage across the state. In letters sent to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton on Oct. 13 and Oct. 21, Republican state Rep. Jeff Leach requested the state government open an investigation into the mailers’ origin.

Sarah Stogner, the district attorney for several West Texas counties, launched a criminal investigation into the materials. Stogner, a Republican, told The Washington Sun that she didn’t “want to speculate” about the campaign, but told the Tribune that mailers were probably sent in an effort to upset voters just before Election Day.

Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee, has repeatedly targeted Democratic nominee James Talarico for his pro-transgender comments throughout the race.

entries.title: RFK Jr. Puts Out a Call to Rebuild the Vaccine Advisory Panel
entries.summary: The solicitation includes broad language that some former members say could allow for people with less vaccine-specific experience to be considered.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is officially seeking new members for the nation’s influential vaccine advisory panel, indicating a renewed effort to remake the group in Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s image.

In a notice posted to the Federal Register on Friday, the Department of Health and Human Services said it is looking for nominations for the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, or ACIP, through Dec. 31. The notice calls for members that “collectively represent a balanced range of scientific, clinical, and public health expertise relevant to the Committee’s mission, including person(s) knowledgeable about consumer perspectives and/or social and community aspects of immunization programs.”

The administration used broader language than previous notices for ACIP nominations have used — subtle changes that some former members say could make it easier for the administration to nominate vaccine skeptics.

Unlike the 2024 call for nominations, the administration’s notice does not include language about vaccine-specific experience. Previous postings have described ACIP members as “experts in fields associated with immunization practices and public health,” followed by a list of vaccine-related areas of expertise.

“You can have people with significant expertise who meet these criteria who are skeptical about vaccines, and their skepticism would not be a disqualifying factor,” said Dr. Jamie Loehr, a family physician, who served on ACIP from 2021 until he was fired from the committee in 2025.

Kennedy fired all 17 members of ACIP in June 2025 and attempted to install new members, including many with a history of vaccine skepticism. The new committee tried to cut the number of recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11.

The actions spurred a lawsuit from the American Public Health Association and medical associations, which claimed that Kennedy did not follow proper procedure in soliciting new nominees. ACIP has not met for nearly a year due to this litigation.

HHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the changes in solicitation language.

While former members are optimistic about ACIP’s return, especially in the midst of the largest measles outbreak in 35 years, some saw the changes in solicitation language as unusual.

“I think this is very concerning,” said Dr. Edwin Asturias, a pediatric infectious-disease specialist and ACIP member from 2024 to 2025. “You wouldn’t want someone without heart expertise making recommendations about heart disease. So why would we accept less clarity about the expertise of the committee making national vaccine recommendations?”

The committee has typically included at least one consumer advocate, according to former ACIP members who spoke to The Washington Sun. However, solicitations for ACIP usually prioritize other areas above consumer advocacy.

Other changes in language also indicate the administration is taking a broader approach. The solicitation says the administration would consider non-U.S. citizens on a case-by-case basis. Older postings have required nominees to be U.S. citizens.

In addition, the 2026 notice leaves out specific language from past notices stating that vaccines recommended by ACIP will be covered under the Affordable Care Act, though coverage for children's vaccines are protected by law.

Kennedy’s past calls for greater research into potential adverse effects of vaccines, as well as the panel’s attempts to loosen recommendations for the children’s vaccine schedule, has made public health experts and former ACIP members nervous about any possible changes to ACIP.

“The administration has been eager to advance unproven theories that undermine proven vaccine safety with untruths and innuendo,” Dr. Noel Brewer, a vaccine and medical researcher at the University of North Carolina, who was on ACIP from 2024 to 2025, said of language in the notice that asked for nominees interested in “identifying areas where additional data or evaluation would inform future recommendations.”

Still, they hope the committee will continue to recruit the expertise required for vaccine recommendations.

“We don’t need a fair balance between well-established evidence and unsupported claims, right?” Asturias said. “So we would like a committee that is laser-focused on making the right decisions for those recommendations to be the best for the American public.”

entries.title: Republicans Kneecapped the FEC. Now the NRSC Wants It to Investigate Mary Peltola.
entries.summary: The GOP’s Senate campaign arm wants Mary Peltola investigated, but Senate Republicans have spent months stalling commission appointments to meet quorum.
entries.content:
The National Republican Senatorial Committee filed a complaint with the Federal Election Commission on Friday, asking the panel to investigate Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s role in an alleged scheme to recruit a candidate with the same name as her opponent.

Peltola campaign staffers and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee reportedly organized to scout another Dan Sullivan to run against incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) — allegations the parties involved deny.

In the seven-page letter to the FEC, first reported by Semafor, Republicans asked the federal elections watchdog to pursue the claims identified in The New York Times article. The letter also includes allegations that Peltola’s camp violated campaign finance law when it coordinated $1.5 million to boost a fourth candidate, Republican Gerald Heikes.

However, the FEC has been effectively shut down for 18 months due to Republican gridlocking.

The federal watchdog tasked with regulating political spending still lacks the four commissioners needed at minimum to establish a quorum necessary to investigate campaign finance complaints.

President Donald Trump declined to appoint nominees that would allow the bipartisan agency to regain its quorum for over nine months since the panel lost quorum in April 2025. In February, he finally named a pair of Republicans to serve on the commission alongside two remaining Democrats. But Senate Republicans tasked with confirming the duo have not moved forward with nomination proceedings, citing paperwork issues and the monthslong medical absence of Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky).

Now, the NRSC is petitioning the commission to investigate the Democrats’ involvement in the alleged efforts to scout Daniel J. Sullivan, a candidate who will appear on the general election ballot next week — despite the lack of quorum.

“The Commission should investigate the facts reported in the NYT Report, sanction to the fullest extent of the law all violations that it finds, and impose such additional remedies as are necessary and appropriate to ensure compliance with the Act,” the letter says, referring to the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971.

Top Republicans also accused the DSCC of improperly directing political payments and asked the FEC to refer its findings to the Department of Justice.

The hobbled commission already presides over a backlog of hundreds of pending enforcement matters, according to FEC Chair Shana Broussard.

Even without a quorum, FEC lawyers will review the complaint and prepare it for the commission's consideration, Tom Moore, a former chief of staff to FEC Commissioner Ellen L. Weintraub, told The Washington Sun. The team will examine whether parties properly disclosed money spent to potentially influence the election and whether any spending involved prohibited coordination.

The process could ultimately take months and would conclude well after Election Day. Recruiting a candidate based on their name is not itself illegal, Moore said. While the financial allegations behind that effort — assertions that Peltola’s campaign illegally coordinated a PAC’s outside spending — could violate campaign finance law, the FEC has historically never punished candidates accused of coordination.

“That is something the Republican commissioners have blocked for years and years,” Moore said.

entries.title: Roger Marshall Hit With Class-Action Lawsuit Over ‘Aggressive’ Medical Billing Practices
entries.summary: The Kansas Republican is accused of forcing patients to pay over 18% in interest, a sum that they claim violated state law.
entries.content:
A former patient of U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, a former OBGYN, is suing him for allegedly overcharging her interest on an overdue medical bill, which she says violated Kansas law.

Meischa Zimmerman filed a class-action lawsuit against the Kansas Republican on Thursday, accusing the senator of forcing patients to pay over 18% in interest rates, a sum they claim violated state law.

The lawsuit, which was also filed “on behalf of” Marshall’s other patients, argues that many of his patients were economically disadvantaged pregnant women and mothers who lived in a rural area with above-average poverty levels.

“Many of Marshall's patients did not have health insurance or had insurance with high deductibles and co-pays that did not pay all the amounts Marshall charged them,” the lawsuit says. “Many were reported as having to decide between paying medical bills or buying groceries.”

The lawsuit dropped just days before the midterm elections, which have become a referendum on the economy in which “affordability” is a major buzzword. Kansas is one of several states where the political landscape has shifted toward Democrats, making the traditional GOP stronghold a battleground state that could decide which party takes control of the Senate.

The New York Times reported last month that Marshall’s practice sued 700 former patients, including new and expectant mothers, to collect on unpaid bills. The damages sought ranged from $101 to thousands of dollars.

This “aggressive” approach continued even as Marshall became a congressman, the lawsuit says, claiming that Marshall’s decision to charge patients 18% interest was “unmitigated greed and blatantly unlawful.”

Kansas prohibits charging more than 15% interest, according to the suit. And when Marshall’s practice was unable to collect, his attorneys requested arrest warrants that led to the arrest of 81 patients.

Zimmerman, the plaintiff in the suit, was arrested three times over $3,596 in unpaid medical bills for the birth of her child in 2009.

In December of that year, Marshall’s practice filed a petition against her in the district court of Barton County to collect the amount plus 18% interest and court costs.

“It could be fully expected that doctors in Kansas would be law-abiding and would not charge their patients unlawful, usurious interest rates,” the lawsuit says. “Only Marshall defied that expectation.”

The lawsuit further accuses Marshall of violating his fiduciary duty by benefiting himself to the detriment of his patients and fraudulently concealing that he charged patients more in interest than he should have under Kansas law.

While the complaint does not request a specific dollar amount, Zimmerman is seeking damages and/or restitution in an amount to be determined at trial, pre- and post-judgment interest, and other types of relief the court considers just and proper.

The Washington Sun has emailed Marshall for comment.

entries.title: Coinbase Scored Another Federal Contract. Does That Make Its Campaign Contributions Illegal?
entries.summary: Since 2024, the FEC has failed to rule on a complaint against Coinbase, which says it’s done nothing wrong.
entries.content:
The U.S. Marshals Service awarded Coinbase an $8.1 million, no-bid contract last month to manage forfeited cryptocurrency, according to a federal contracting document released this week.

Federal government contractors are generally not allowed to donate to political committees. But Coinbase, the largest U.S.-based crypto exchange, is one of the nation’s most prolific corporate political donors.

Coinbase received a $30 million-plus contract in 2024 to manage seized cryptocurrency assets for the Marshals Service, the federal law enforcement agency that handles asset forfeiture. The Marshals Service moved quickly this fall to give Coinbase the new federal contract following a major scandal involving another contractor, Command Services and Support Inc., which had also received a crypto management contract in 2024.

In January 2026, the Marshals Service discovered that the son of the company president had stolen at least $46 million from wallets managed by the agency, according to a redacted justification document written by the agency and signed affidavit by an FBI special agent.

“The USMS is now facing an emergent and urgent situation that requires an immediate solution in order to avoid further possible loss of seized cryptocurrency,” the agency wrote in a redacted justification document arguing Coinbase is the only suitable company to take over the contract.

The value of the digital assets Coinbase would manage under the contract is redacted, but the document describes the inventory as “sizable.”

Marshals Service spokesperson Abigail Meyer declined to comment beyond the information in the contract. Meyer also said The Washington Sun must file a Freedom of Information Act request for the inventory balance.

Coinbase did not respond to requests for comment.In recent years, Coinbase has spent massive amounts of money on federal elections.

During the 2024 election cycle, Coinbase gave more than $79 million to federal political committees, including the pro-crypto super PAC Fairshake, according to campaign finance data analyzed by OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan nonprofit that tracks the flow of money in American politics.
Coinbase.CEO.Trump (4392x2928, AR: 1.50)Coinbase has continued to spend tens of millions of dollars during the 2026 election cycle, including more than $52.5 million in contributions to Fairshake, according to Federal Election Commission data.

Left-leaning nonprofit watchdog Public Citizen argues that Coinbase is breaking the law with its contributions.

After Coinbase received the first Marshal Service contract in 2024, Public Citizen filed a complaint with the FEC accusing Coinbase of violating a ban on political contributions by federal contractors.

A few days out from the 2026 general election, the FEC has still not ruled on whether Coinbase is violating the ban.

Two factors contribute to the delay.

First, under the best of circumstances, it can take months or even years for the FEC to investigate complaints.

Second, since May 2025, the FEC has not had enough commissioners to carry out any of its high-level duties — including investigations and enforcement actions — because the Senate has yet to vote on a pair of commissioner candidates President Donald Trump nominated in February, months after the agency dipped below its quorum of four commissioners.

The FEC’s enforcement backlog has ballooned to more than 300 cases, FEC Chair Shana Broussard wrote on Bluesky last month.

In response to questions about the status of the Public Citizen complaint, Myles Martin, a spokesperson for the FEC, told The Sun there were no closed cases involving Coinbase in the agency’s enforcement database.

Rick Claypool, a research director at Public Citizen, and Molly White, an independent researcher who filed the complaint with Public Citizen, said they’ve heard no update from the FEC on the status of their complaint against Coinbase.

“The fact that Coinbase has spent another, you know, $60-plus million since the complaint was received by the FEC certainly suggests that they're not in any hurry to stop the spending,” White told The Sun.

The company has previously denied it’s in violation of the federal contractor contribution ban.

“Whether intentional or not, this is misinformation,” Paul Grewal, then-chief legal officer at Coinbase, wrote in a post on X in 2024, arguing Coinbase was not a contractor “under the plain language” of the law.

Federal law defines a government contractor as anyone who enters into a contract paid “in whole or in part from funds appropriated by the Congress.” Since the contract is funded by the Justice Department’s Asset Forfeiture Fund, rather than traditional, annual congressional appropriations, the ban does not apply, Grewal argued.

Meyer, the Marshals Service spokesperson, confirmed the contract was funded by the forfeiture fund.

White and Public Citizen pushed back in a supplemental memo to the FEC that summer, arguing the law does not specify traditional, annual appropriation funding and that Congress itself established the Asset Forfeiture Fund.

“If their interpretation is accurate, then there's a huge loophole in these laws where … basically anyone could argue that they're not a federal contractor,” White told The Sun. “I think that it's just not an accurate interpretation, and they pretty clearly are a federal contractor.”

Eric Petry, counsel in the Brennan Center for Justice's elections and government program, told The Sun that this “really technical difference” in the legal wording, which he interprets as “only applies to contractors who are paid from funds appropriated by Congress,” is just one more example of why Congress should expand the scope of its federal contractor contribution ban.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) and Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California) told The Sun this week that they plan to introduce a bill aimed at another major political donor, Elon Musk, whose companies receive billions in government contracts. The bill would extend the federal contribution ban to include executive officeholders, shareholders and affiliated corporations of government contractors.

Petry called it “tremendously exciting” to see the legislation introduced and a “step in the right direction.”

But he expressed frustration that the FEC has been unable to address a complaint made during the 2024 election cycle before Election Day 2026.

“It's bad enough when the laws are weak or there are loopholes in the law, but it's almost worse when you have laws on the books that aren't being enforced because the regulator is inadequate, and that's the situation where we're finding ourselves now,” Petry said.

entries.title: DOJ Urges Judge to Allow a Third Comey Charge
entries.summary: An attorney for the former FBI director argued that prosecutors needed to obtain a grand jury indictment already.
entries.content:
A federal judge in Washington on Friday sounded open to allowing the Trump administration’s third and latest criminal case against James Comey to proceed so a grand jury can decide whether to indict the former FBI director.

The Justice Department sought to charge Comey with Espionage Act violations, alleging he illegally disclosed national defense information to The New York Times in 2016. But prosecutors did not secure a grand jury indictment within a 10-year statute of limitations.

Instead, DOJ officials this week unsealed criminal information — a charging document with a lower legal threshold — seeking to preserve their ability to prosecute him.

Comey’s lawyers are challenging the unusual move, arguing that prosecutors were required to obtain an indictment to keep the clock running.

Judge Trevor McFadden questioned why he shouldn’t simply allow grand jurors to continue weighing evidence in the case and see if they issue an indictment. They may ultimately refuse, he said.

“It turns out ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days,” McFadden commented, referencing a well-worn legal expression that a grand jury would indict a ham sandwich if asked.

Comey’s attorney, Ephraim McDowell, said the government had a decade to pursue charges and “waited until the last minute” after the statute of limitations had expired.

“The time has come to an end,” he told the judge.

Allowing the charges to linger while grand jurors deliberate would be unfair to Comey, McDowell said. He said FBI agents had appeared outside Comey’s home.

“That’s a real threat that has been hanging over Mr. Comey,” McDowell said. “He should get to rest and not face the possibility of criminal charges.”

McFadden stopped short of ruling from the bench, but gave the government a firm warning while he considers his next steps.

“I will be extremely frustrated,” he said, “if there’s some sort of dawn raid or black pajamas turning up outside Mr. Comey’s home.”

The government’s lawyer, Dustin Farahnak, responded, “That’s not going to happen.”

Much of Friday’s hearing centered on whether federal law permits the DOJ to substitute a criminal information — which does not require a finding of probable cause — for a grand jury indictment.

Farahnak told the judge that they were essentially the same legal tools for the purposes of this case. He pushed back on the defense’s argument that prosecutors had waited too long, saying they had found new evidence and needed time to present.

“We had a clock problem with a complex and important case, and we looked at the law, and we followed it,” Farahnak said.

The crimes alleged in the government’s two-count indictment date back to Oct. 5. The government filed the criminal information under seal exactly 10 years later to the day.

Farahnak said grand jurors were still considering evidence and that prosecutors were “still going to the grand jury diligently.”

He said he didn’t think the proceedings would harm Comey, contending that the case was not an “abusive hypothetical where a defendant has an indictment hanging over their head.”

Comey is facing a separate federal charge in North Carolina over a social media post that prosecutors say constituted a threat against the president’s life. A federal judge last year threw out another indictment accusing Comey of lying to Congress.
