entries.title: Negotiations Are On-Deck to Form Israeli Government As Votes Don't Provide a Majority
entries.summary: After the results are certified and submitted next week, President Isaac Herzog will task someone with forming the new government.
entries.content:
By Cara Anna and Ibrahim Hazboun

Israel's final election results confirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority and that weeks of difficult negotiations among very different parties, from ultra-Orthodox Jewish to secular to Arab-led, lie ahead.

The results released early Friday showed Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday's election. The main opposition bloc won 48. Arab-led parties secured the other 19, a historic showing. Now parties must meet, bargain and seek a way to team up for at least 61 seats in the 120-member Knesset.

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, remains in charge. His main opponents would most likely need to partner with the Arab-led parties to replace him.

Underscoring the fraught path ahead, Avigdor Lieberman, the leader of a right-wing anti-Netanyahu faction, on Friday appeared to rule out any partnership with Arab-led parties. That alone would make it nearly impossible for Netanyahu’s opponents to form a coalition to oust him.

Difficult decisions lie ahead. Will the main opposition parties that campaigned hard to unseat the divisive Netanyahu make the politically sensitive choice to partner with Arab-led ones? Or will they toss their vows aside to team up with Netanyahu in a potentially fractious unity government?

Israel largely shuts down on Friday for the Jewish Sabbath, and it was not clear who might be meeting with whom. Israelis debated possible coalitions and challenges, as some expressed traditional wariness around Arab parties and others insisted it was time for Jewish-led parties to embrace them.

The election results still need to be certified and submitted to the president next Wednesday. Then President Isaac Herzog will task someone with forming the new government. That could be the leader of the party that received the most votes — Netanyahu — or whoever leaders of the various parties believe is best suited.

If multiple attempts to form a government fail, Israel faces a new election early next year. Herzog this week said he will do everything in his power to avoid that scenario.

entries.title: Judge Launches Investigation Into Trump Officials In East Potomac Renovation Case
entries.summary: Judge Ana Reyes said either she or a "special master" will probe whether officials committed misconduct in her courtroom.
entries.content:
A Trump administration official said Friday that renovation plans for East Potomac Golf Links had been in the works for weeks, prompting a federal judge to open an official investigation into attorney misconduct.

Judge Ana Reyes often aired frustration and exasperation at the court hearing, where Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward told her an official at the Interior Department had “put pen to paper” on a plan to redevelop the golf course in recent weeks.

Woodward, the No. 3 official at DOJ, had told the court in an Oct. 19 hearing that there were no plans to close the course for redevelopment by Nov. 15, a day after President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the course would close for restoration by then.

Reyes called for the hearing after yet another Trump post on Monday that said “we are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th.”

The president’s use of the words “as scheduled” indicated there were concrete plans for the site — despite the government’s refusal to detail plans in court earlier in the month.

Reyes expressed disbelief that no one had mentioned the active planning at that previous hearing, and she called for a 15-minute break after learning the news.

“Are you telling the court there’s been pen to paper for plans to redevelop the East Potomac golf course in the last two weeks, and no one, no one mentioned that on Oct. 19 in a seven-hour meeting?” Reyes asked.

Reyes had called the hearing and ordered Woodward to appear, demanding to know more about Trump’s announcement on social media and whether the government had run afoul of her order requiring official notice before moving forward with the project.

By the end, Reyes said she would launch an investigation into whether Trump administration officials committed misconduct in her courtroom, including Woodward. Reyes said she will either appoint a "special master" or do the investigation herself.

That would likely include questioning DOJ and Interior Department lawyers, a mini-trial with an evidentiary hearing and possible sanctions against government officials. The judge said she's looking into whether government lawyers lied to the court or failed to correct past statements about what the Trump administration is planning to do with the public golf course on the Potomac River.

That includes whether the government held back notice about cutting down trees "to intentionally evade judicial review" and hide it from her, whether lawyers instructed officials to leave out details in court filings, and whether lawyers were being truthful when they said there were no plans to redesign the golf course.

The government has five business days to object to the appointment of a special master. Reyes told the court the formal inquiry does not mean the court has found evidence of unethical misconduct.

"That's why we're conducting an investigation," she said.

The skirmish on Friday followed an atypical series of events, in which the president of the United States took particular interest in the redevelopment of a municipal golf course, the No. 3 at the DOJ became personally involved by defending it — and the government tried to get the judge to remove herself from the case.

Earlier in the hearing, when Reyes asked for clarity on what the president meant when he said the course would close on Nov. 15, Woodward stonewalled — prompting rebukes and gasps of incredulity from the judge and repeated reminders of his duties as a lawyer.

“I don't know what the president meant, and if I did, I couldn't talk about that,” he replied.

When she pressed further, Woodward sought to shut down the inquiry by pointing to a presidential power to keep certain information private: “That seems to fall squarely within executive privilege.”

“He posted it publicly!” Reyes said.

Reyes at one point reminded Woodward of his “duty to make reasonable inquiry” before making representations in court and his responsibility to “ensure the truth to the court,” going so far as to read him the D.C. bar rules.

When Woodward indicated that tree removal — which she has already paused — was part of a plan, she read back his statements to ask whether the government had been hiding information from her.

And when she probed the government’s claims that renovation is necessary to build a seawall for the supposed safety of golfers, Reyes chuckled and asked Woodward if he’d ever even been there.

“You think there's a danger of people falling into the Potomac? Just flinging themselves off?” she said.

“What's the safety issue with the seawall?” Reyes asked.

“The pictures speak for themselves,” Woodward replied.

“No, they don't. What's the safety issue?” she asked again.

Woodward repeated his line about the pictures several more times — then attempted to end the back-and-forth. “I don’t know why this is an effective line of inquiry,” he said.

“I get to decide what the effective line of inquiry is,” the judge shot back.

When Woodward seemed annoyed at the way the inquiry was going, Reyes made clear she’d run out of patience as well.

“I imagine that the third-highest ranking DOJ official has more important things to do than talk about a golf course,” she said, cautioning him to avoid grumbling about a Friday hearing. “Do that over drinks with your friends.”

entries.title: Park Police Pursuit Ends in a Crash for the Third Time This Week
entries.summary: Policies for Park Police car chases were loosened last year under an executive order from President Donald Trump.
entries.content:
For the third time this week, a car chase involving U.S. Park Police in D.C. ended in a collision late Thursday.

Two earlier chases on Monday and Tuesday ended in collisions in Indian Head, Maryland, and near the White House, respectively. The collisions were first reported by WUSA9.

U.S. Park Police pursued a driver across town in the Thursday chase, a USPP spokesperson said in a statement to The Washington Sun.

The spokesperson said that just before midnight, USPP attempted a traffic stop on a vehicle “being operated recklessly” in the area of H and 11th Streets NE and pursued the vehicle when the driver did not stop. The driver, who has not been identified, struck a light pole near the intersection of Georgia Avenue and Fern Street NW before being arrested and taken to a hospital for non-life-threatening injuries.

On Monday night, officers pursued a driver with an active warrant for assault with a deadly weapon, USPP said in a statement. That driver also fled the scene and struck another vehicle in Indian Head, Maryland, according to USPP. The suspect was taken into custody and treated at a local hospital for non-life-threatening injuries.

USPP said in a statement that officers attempted another traffic stop for reckless driving early Tuesday. That driver sped away from the traffic stop and lost control of their vehicle before striking a building near the White House. Both occupants of the vehicle were detained after attempting to flee the scene and were taken to a hospital for non-life-threatening injuries. One occupant was in possession of a controlled substance, USPP said.

Policies for USPP car chases were loosened recently. Last year, President Donald Trump issued an executive order allowing USPP to conduct vehicular pursuits if suspects were wanted for or suspected of felony offenses or if a threat to the general public existed.

The previous policy allowed pursuit of a vehicle only when the suspect was wanted for a violent felony offense or if the person had committed a felony and was in possession of a firearm.

The new policy drew criticism when a delivery driver was killed after being struck by a vehicle involved in a USPP pursuit in June.

A spokesperson for Mayor Muriel Bowser declined to comment and referred The Sun to Park Police. When asked for comment, the Metropolitan Police Department directed The Sun to USPP.

entries.title: Elon Musk, ‘Dark Money’ Help Fuel Record Spending in 2026 Midterms
entries.summary: OpenSecrets predicts the midterms will cost $11.9 billion at the federal level.
entries.content:
The campaign finance research organization OpenSecrets is projecting a gargantuan final price tag for the 2026 elections: $11.9 billion, a record for any midterm, according to a new analysis released Friday evening.

Adjusted for inflation, that’s $1.7 billion more than the 2022 elections, OpenSecrets found, crediting a rise in outside spending by super PACs.

“When all the reporting is in, we will have another record midterm election,” OpenSecrets’ staff wrote in their report.

More than $445 million came from one man: Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and a key ally of President Donald Trump.

Other nine-figure political donors this election cycle include Michael Bloomberg, Richard Uihlein and Jeffrey Yass.

OpenSecrets said about $1.5 billion worth of spending during the 2026 midterms has already come from “dark money” — money that can’t be traced to a root source.

entries.title: Trump Lawyers Call His Arch a High Priority. Some Veterans Call It Disrespectful.
entries.summary: A judge said she will rule “expeditiously” on whether the project can proceed and whether the veterans have standing to pursue the case.
entries.content:
Michael Lemmon didn’t get a celebratory welcome back to D.C. when he returned from the Vietnam War in 1970. He still grapples with how that felt, even 56 years later.

He often visits Arlington National Cemetery to pay respect to his fellow soldiers. Some days, he walks from his home in D.C. to the Vietnam War Memorial to see the names of his friends on the granite wall. From there, he makes the short trek to the Lincoln Memorial to look over at the cemetery — the final resting place of his comrades, and the place he plans to be buried.

“I personally feel the hurt, the anger … the trauma recede” when he looks over the cemetery, he said during a court hearing Friday. “It means an immense amount to me to be able to do that.”

In what she acknowledged as an unusual move, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan allowed Lemmon to give a short testimony as she considered whether to stop construction of President Donald Trump’s proposed 250-foot arch, which will obstruct the line of sight between the National Mall and the cemetery. Those hearings are usually limited to arguments from lawyers and questions from the presiding judge.

Lemmon and two fellow Vietnam War veterans filed a lawsuit in February to prevent construction of the arch, arguing that the administration sidestepped congressional approval and that the arch would impede the peaceful atmosphere of the cemetery. Lawyers for the three men asked Chukan, an Obama appointee, to issue a preliminary injunction, arguing in court documents that no harm will come to the government if excavation work is postponed.

Trump administration lawyers on Friday argued the arch is a “high-priority project” and that any postponement would be a “serious infringement on the work of the federal government.”

Robert Stander, deputy assistant attorney general, propped the arch up as a matter of national security at the hearing, referring to recent court affidavits filed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin that imply plans to use the arch as a drone defense facility.

“This is a very serious business,” Stander said at the hearing. “We all know there have been assasination attempts on the president. … The arch is a generational national defense opportunity.”

Stander did not answer questions from Chutkan about assertions that the arch would support military operations as outlined in the affidavits.

Chutkan pushed back on the government's national security justification, which was mentioned in court filings for the first time on Thursday. She said plans to use the arch, which the government has also touted as a tourist destination expected to draw 2,000 to 22,000 daily visitors, for military purposes raises many questions.

Chutkan said she would rule “expeditiously” on whether the project can proceed. She is also expected to rule on whether the three veterans have the standing to pursue the case.

Stander argued the veterans' objections rested solely upon being offended and disgusted by what the arch stands for, which is not enough of a legal standing to prove real harm and thus grounds for dismissal of the case.

Wendy Liu, a lawyer representing the veterans, said the government’s argument diminished the experience of the veterans who often visit the graves of their friends at Arlington National Cemetery. Each has experienced “profound and personal” moments while paying their respects, which would be “personally taken away” by the arch’s looming presence, Liu said.

For Lemmon, beyond the obstructed view of the cemetery, lawyers argued the arch would put a shadow over a grave he visits often, casting some of his visits in darkness. Lemmon called the planned monument “disrespectful” to what he considers the “sacred territory” of the cemetery.

“The pain is real. The pain is real for us veterans. It's not just some aesthetic, not just some preference for a view,” he said.” “It is deep in our memory and remembrance.”

entries.title: DOJ Sends Letters Threatening Election Officials Over Records Preservation
entries.summary: The department sent letters Thursday to officials in all 50 states, threatening criminal prosecution if they don’t preserve records connected to next week’s elections.
entries.content:
The Justice Department warned election officials from all 50 states that they could face criminal charges if they fail to preserve certain Election Day materials like ballots and voter rolls for the next two years.

The letters, sent Thursday and signed by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, are at least the third instance of members of President Donald Trump’s administration promising aggressive legal intervention if state officials don’t comply with federal elections-related requests.

The letters warn that it is unlawful to willfully steal, destroy, conceal, mutilate or alter election records — adding that violations are punishable by up to a year in prison.

In July, the department told states that election officials would face criminal liability if they allow noncitizens to vote, which is already rare and illegal. DOJ officials last month sent officials similar letters, threatening those who fail to preserve records from the 2024 election.

States hold authority over the federal government to conduct their own elections.

The Trump administration has demanded California officials segregate ballots from 20,000 voters the government has flagged as potential noncitizens and issued grand jury subpoenas to several local officials. Officials in Washington state this week similarly received letters asking them to segregate ballots, a request the state’s secretary of state said was based on inaccurate information.

entries.title: Appeals Court Keeps Restrictions on DHS’s Door-Knocking Voter Investigations
entries.summary: A three-judge panel called the timing of the preelection surge “questionable.”
entries.content:
A federal appellate court on Friday upheld a lower court order that restricted Department of Homeland Security agents from door-knocking at homes of citizens as part of the preelection voter fraud probe in nine states.

A three-judge panel of the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals declined to lift a block on DHS agents conducting elections-related operations targeting people as part of the Trump administration’s initiative to find suspected illegal voting by noncitizens. The block, which is in effect until polls close on Election Day, is meant to protect naturalized citizens from voter intimidation.

The panel pointed to DHS’s timing of the operations and its delay in court action as reasons why keeping the restrictions in place would not harm the government, as the DOJ had argued.

“The Federal Defendants’ questionable timing in pursuing a ‘surge’ in voter fraud enforcement operations, and Federal Defendants’ delay in seeking a stay further undermine any potential showing of irreparable harm,” the court’s order states. “In an operation ostensibly focused on past voter fraud, the government could have aggressively pursued its campaign against non-citizen voting well before these elections commenced.”

Voter rights groups and local governments in California sued DHS last month over its deployment of agents to question people at their homes in search of noncitizen voters. The door-knocking operation by armed officials and the publicization of those operations and arrests amounted to voter intimidation, the groups and local officials argued.

The 9th Circuit ruling comes as legal battles are developing across the country in the days ahead of the election, with the Trump administration seeking to prove that immigration-related voter fraud is taking place at a wide scale.

“Last week, the district court held that DHS's frantic, last-minute voter investigations are unlawful voter intimidation,” said Beau Tremitiere, an attorney from Protect Democracy, representing the plaintiffs. “Today, the government's attempt to restart that campaign failed.”

The prohibition on the field operations only applies to California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington state and Wisconsin, where DHS directed Homeland Security Investigations agents to prioritize questioning people about their voter eligibility based on data that includes naturalized citizens.

During a hearing Thursday, the judges questioned the Justice Department attorney about why the government would be harmed if it couldn’t continue its investigation until after Election Day.

“You can't prosecute anybody in four days; you can't convict them in four days,” Judge Sidney Thomas said. “Why do you need these four days to complete your tasks?”

DOJ attorney Gabriel Schonfeld replied that he couldn’t give specifics of any investigation and asked for a narrower bar that would only apply to naturalized citizens.

“The government can't tell today what conduct would result in contempt, the government is being chilled,” Schonfeld said.

Earlier in the hearing Judge Kim McLane Wardlaw highlighted the unreliability of the data being used to target people. A whistleblower report to Congress last month said that U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’s search for evidence of noncitizen voting swept in foreign-born citizens without reliable data on whether they had voted prior to their naturalization.

“That's not really in debate that naturalized citizens are being targeted, and plaintiffs are fearful of that,” said Hayden Johnson, the attorney representing the California Nurses Association, the San Francisco city and county governments, Santa Clara County, National Nurses United and the Voto Latino Foundation.

A different panel of the same appellate court this week dismissed another emergency request from the Trump administration, which is seeking the sequestering of 20,000 mail ballots from people suspected of voting without citizenship.

entries.title: RNC Sues Iowa Election Official for Access to Voting Machine ID Numbers
entries.summary: The party’s public-records lawsuit comes days before the midterms, amid broader Republican efforts to scrutinize voting equipment and voter eligibility.
entries.content:
The Republican National Committee sued an Iowa election official Thursday for access to voting machine data, escalating a fight over how much access third-party monitors should have to election records five days before the midterms.

The lawsuit, filed in a Black Hawk County district court, alleges County Auditor Karen Showalter broke the law by stopping RNC observers from writing down or photographing the serial numbers on plastic security seals used to lock voting machines after they are tested.

“The seal permits the commissioner and the public to determine that the tabulating equipment has not been altered between testing and its use in the election,” the RNC wrote. “The defendant refused to permit RNC representatives to photograph or otherwise document the seal numbers placed on tabulating equipment.”

Showalter and county officials say keeping serial numbers secret is vital to protecting machines from being hacked. They maintain that state laws permit them to shield critical infrastructure from the public.

The party is asking a judge to force the county to hand over the seal logs, fine the auditor and pay for the RNC’s legal bills.

The case comes as President Donald Trump’s administration pursues litigation concerning voting equipment and voter eligibility across the country. Thursday’s complaint argues that voting machine serial numbers should be available for public inspection, despite the fact that the digits are intentionally obscured to prevent unwanted tampering.

Republicans have increasingly sought to discontinue the use of QR-code-based voting machines ahead of November’s election, as widespread conspiracy theories conjure fears about foreign interference.

The testing is legal under Iowa law, the complaint asserts.

Members of the public interested in testing voting machines are required by law to sign a certificate documenting that the machines were securely sealed, though the statute does not require listing the digits on the seals — just the serial numbers and locations of the devices being tested.

Showalter cited state security exemptions and a 2018 county resolution to justify her refusal to grant the RNC access, according to an email cited in the complaint.
